Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and let $\delta\in R$. The object labels are the nonnegative integers $n=0,1,2,\ldots$. For labels $m,n$, place bottom points $b_1,\ldots,b_m$ and top points $t_1,\ldots,t_n$ along the rectangle from left to right on their respective edges. Their cyclic order is $t_1,\ldots,t_n,b_m,\ldots,b_1$. When $m=n=0$, the empty matching is included.

An $(m,n)$ **diagram** is a perfect matching of these $m+n$ boundary labels which is noncrossing: there are no four labels $a,b,c,d$ in cyclic order whose matched pairs are $\{a,c\}$ and $\{b,d\}$. A picture consists of disjoint arcs realizing the matching; equality is equality of the matching, so planar deformation that fixes the boundary does not change a diagram. If $m+n$ is odd, there are no such diagrams. Write $\mathcal D(m,n)$ for this set and define the $R$-module

$$M_R(m,n):=R^{(\mathcal D(m,n))},$$

the free $R$-module on the set of diagrams ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]). In particular, its diagram basis is empty when $m+n$ is odd.

For basis diagrams $D:m\to n$ and $E:n\to p$, stack $E$ above $D$ and identify the $n$ matching boundary points. The resulting finite graph has degree two at each identified point, where degree means the number of incident arcs. Each component is a path joining two exterior boundary points or a closed cycle. Remove every cycle and multiply the remaining exterior matching by $\delta^c$, where $c$ is the number of removed cycles. Denote this output by $E\circ D$ and extend the rule $R$-bilinearly to a map $M_R(n,p)\times M_R(m,n)\to M_R(m,p)$. A following result proves closure of these operations on the diagram modules and the category axioms.

The matching $1_n:n\to n$ pairs each bottom point to the top point directly above it. Horizontal juxtaposition, with the left diagram placed first, defines $m\otimes m'=m+m'$ on object labels and $D\otimes D'$ on basis diagrams; extend it $R$-bilinearly to the modules. A following result proves that these operations give a strict monoidal category.

For $1\le i<n$, let $d_i\in M_R(n,n)$ be the diagram with a cap joining top points $i,i+1$, a cup joining bottom points $i,i+1$, and vertical through strands at every other position. Define $\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$ to be the $R$-module $M_R(n,n)$ with bilinear multiplication $xy:=x\circ y$ and distinguished element $1_n$. A following result proves that it is a unital associative $R$-algebra and identifies it with the endomorphism algebra at object $n$.

The left factor is stacked above the right factor. The loop value is $\delta$; no invertibility or nonzero condition on $\delta$ is part of these data.

For every commutative ring $R$, loop value $\delta\in R$, and objects $m,n,p,q\ge0$, the raw diagram data of [[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-category]] form a strict monoidal category $\mathcal{TL}_R(\delta)$ with hom-modules $M_R(m,n)$ and the stated $R$-bilinear stacking composition. Composition is associative, the identity diagrams are two-sided identities, and horizontal juxtaposition is a strict monoidal bifunctor with unit object $0$. Consequently $\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{TL}_R(\delta)}(n)=\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$ is a unital associative $R$-algebra whose underlying $R$-module is free on its noncrossing pairing diagrams.

For every $n\ge0$, each basis diagram in $\mathcal D(n,n)$ is a finite product of the elementary diagrams $d_1,\ldots,d_{n-1}$ from [[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-category]]. The product can be chosen so that no intermediate stack creates a closed cycle. Therefore the set of diagrams lies in the unital subalgebra of $\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$ generated by these diagrams.

Put $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ and $\delta=q+q^{-1}$. For a commutative $A$-algebra $R$, let $V_n$ be the free $R$-module on binary words of length $n$, with $V_0=R$. The cup and cap maps are

$$c(1)=q(01)+(10),\qquad b(01)=1,\quad b(10)=q^{-1},\quad b(00)=b(11)=0.$$

Insertion of these maps in adjacent positions defines a representation

$$\rho_n:\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)\longrightarrow\operatorname{End}_R(V_n).$$

Over $A$ this map has an $A$-linear left inverse, and the same left inverse works after every base change to $R$. In particular, it is injective over every such $R$. It preserves the number of ones, and on the local ordered basis $00,01,10,11$ the generator $d_i$ has zero $00,11$ blocks and middle block

$$\begin{pmatrix}q&1\\1&q^{-1}\end{pmatrix}.$$

Horizontal reflection of an endomorphism diagram is represented by matrix transpose.

For $0\le k\le n$, let $G_{n,k}(Q)$ be the polynomial $\sum_w Q^{\operatorname{inv}(w)}$, summed over binary words with $k$ ones and $n-k$ zeros, where $\operatorname{inv}(w)$ counts pairs with a one to the left of a zero. There is a unique polynomial $B_{n,k}(T)\in\mathbb Z[T]$ such that

$$B_{n,k}(q+q^{-1})=q^{-k(n-k)}G_{n,k}(q^2).$$

It agrees as a rational-function identity with $[n]!/([k]![n-k]!)$; its value at a specialized loop parameter is the polynomial value, without division by vanishing factorials.

For a field $K$, $\delta\in K$, recurrence quantum characteristic $\ell$, and $p=\operatorname{char}K$, every $B_{n,k}(\delta)$ for $0\le k\le n$ is nonzero exactly as follows: if $\ell=\infty$, at every finite $n$; if $\ell<\infty$ and $p>0$, when $n<\ell$ or $n=a\ell p^{i-1}-1$ with $i\ge1$ and $1\le a<p$; if $\ell<\infty$ and $p=0$, when $n<\ell$ or $n=a\ell-1$ for a positive integer $a$.

Let $K$ be a field, $\delta\in K$, and $n\ge0$. A normalized idempotent $e\in\mathrm{TL}_n(K,\delta)$ with $d_ie=0$ for $1\le i<n$ exists if and only if every $B_{n,k}(\delta)$ of [[lem-temperley-lieb-quantum-binomial-digit-criterion]], $0\le k\le n$, is nonzero. Every such $e$ also satisfies $ed_i=0$ and is unique. This is a field assertion; it makes no integral-ring descent claim.

derivations.claim: By propagation in [F1], the span of the nonidentity diagrams is an ideal, so $\varepsilon$ is a ring homomorphism; that ideal is spanned by nonempty generator words. Thus the linear equations $d_ie=0$, $\varepsilon(e)=1$ imply $ae=\varepsilon(a)e$ for every $a$, and in particular $e^2=e$. Horizontal reflection defines an anti-involution $*$ fixing generators and preserving $\varepsilon$. The element $f=ee^*$ is killed by the generators on both sides and has augmentation $1$. Right annihilation gives $fe=f$, while left annihilation of $e$ gives $fe=e$; hence $e=f$ is two-sided. For two such elements $e,e'$, the same argument gives $ee'=e$ by right annihilation of $e$ and $ee'=e'$ by left annihilation of $e'$. They are equal. These arguments use no division and work over every commutative coefficient ring.

First work over any commutative ring $C$ containing a unit $q$ with $\delta=q+q^{-1}$. In the weight-$k$ word module of [F2], the equations for the common kernel are $a_{u10v}=-q a_{u01v}$. Successive adjacent swaps reduce each word to $0^{n-k}1^k$ and change its inversion number by one. Thus this kernel is exactly the free line generated by $v_k=\sum_w(-q)^{\operatorname{inv}(w)}w$, whose baseword coefficient is $1$. If $e$ is normalized, step 1.1 and symmetry in [F2] put both the columns and rows of its weight block in this line. First comparing the baseword column, and then each row, expresses the block as $\alpha_kv_kv_k^{\mathsf T}$ for some $\alpha_k\in C$. Every nonempty generator word kills $v_k$ by its rightmost factor; consequently $(e-1)v_k=0$. Comparing the baseword coefficient in $ev_k=v_k$ gives $\alpha_kG_{n,k}(q^2)=1$. In particular all these Gaussian values are units. This conclusion remains valid with nilpotents or zero divisors.

For general $R$, put $R'=R[q]/(q^2-\delta q+1)$. Division by this monic quadratic gives a unique representative $a+bq$: subtract successive leading terms to prove existence, while a nonzero multiple of a monic polynomial has degree at least two, proving uniqueness. Thus $R'=R\oplus Rq$ as an $R$-module, $R$ injects into $R'$, and $q$ is a unit with inverse $\delta-q$. Base-changing an existing $e$ to $R'$ and applying step 2.1 makes $G_{n,k}(q^2)$ a unit. By [F3] the factor $q^{k(n-k)}$ is a unit, so $B=B_{n,k}(\delta)$ is a unit in $R'$. Write its inverse $a+bq$. The equality $B(a+bq)=1$ in the indicated free basis gives $Ba=1$ in $R$. Hence $B$ is already a unit in $R$.

To prove sufficiency construct a universal projector with only the named denominators. Use an indeterminate $q$, $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$, and its fraction field $L=\mathbb Q(q)$. Facts [F3, F4] give a normalized projector $p\in\mathrm{TL}_n(L,q+q^{-1})$. Step 2.1 determines each of its weight blocks as $v_kv_k^{\mathsf T}/G_{n,k}(q^2)$. Let $S=A[G_{n,k}(q^2)^{-1}:0\le k\le n]\subset L$. That matrix has entries in $S$. Apply the base-changed linear left inverse of [F2] to obtain a diagram-coefficient vector $z\in\mathrm{TL}_n(S,q+q^{-1})$. After extension to $L$ it equals $p$. Since $S$ injects into $L$ and the diagram module is free, the same identities already hold over $S$: $\varepsilon(z)=1$, $d_iz=zd_i=0$ and $z^2=z$. Thus no unproved assertion about the image or centralizer of a quantum-group action is needed.

Suppose now every $B_{n,k}(\delta)$ is a unit in $R$, and form $R'$ as in step 3.1. Fact [F3] makes all evaluated $G_{n,k}(q^2)$ units in $R'$. Therefore evaluation defines a ring homomorphism $S\to R'$: send a fraction $a/\prod G_{n,k}^{e_k}$ to the evaluated numerator times the inverses of the indicated evaluated denominators; the cross-multiplied equality defining equal fractions remains true after evaluation. Specialize $z$ from step 3.2 to get a normalized annihilator $e'\in\mathrm{TL}_n(R',\delta)$. Let $\pi:R'\to R$ be the $R$-linear coefficient projection $\pi(a+bq)=a$ and apply $\pi$ to every diagram coefficient of $e'$, obtaining $e\in\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$. Left multiplication by each $d_i$ has matrix entries in $R$, so it commutes with this coefficient projection. Hence $d_ie=0$ and $\varepsilon(e)=\pi(1)=1$. Step 1.1 now makes $e$ the required unique two-sided idempotent. The projection is used only on these linear equations; it need not preserve multiplication.

Any homomorphism $R\to T$ sends the diagram coefficients and their defining linear identities to those over $T$, so the image of the projector is the unique projector there by step 1.1. For $n=0,1$ there are no generator equations, the identity is the projector, and every binomial in the row is $1$. The same argument includes the zero ring under the convention that its identity is its unique element. This establishes all stated implications and boundaries.

For every $n\ge0$, each basis diagram in $\mathcal D(n,n)$ is a finite product of the elementary diagrams $d_1,\ldots,d_{n-1}$ from [[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-category]]. The product can be chosen so that no intermediate stack creates a closed cycle. Therefore the set of diagrams lies in the unital subalgebra of $\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$ generated by these diagrams.

Fix $n\ge0$, a commutative ring $R$, and $\delta\in R$. For $1\le i<n$, let $d_i\in\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$ be the elementary cup-cap diagram of [[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-category]]. Then

$$d_i^2=\delta d_i,\qquad d_i d_{i+1}d_i=d_i,\qquad d_{i+1}d_i d_{i+1}=d_{i+1},\qquad d_i d_j=d_jd_i\quad(|i-j|>1).$$

Consequently the assignment $u_i\mapsto d_i$ extends to a unital $R$-algebra homomorphism

$$\pi_n:P_n(R,\delta)\longrightarrow\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta).$$

Fix $n\ge0$, a commutative ring $R$, and $\delta\in R$, and use the presented algebra $P_n(R,\delta)$ of [[def-temperley-lieb-generator-presentation]]. For $r\ge0$ and sequences $j_1,\ldots,j_r$ and $k_1,\ldots,k_r$ satisfying

$$1\le k_i\le j_i<n,\qquad j_i<j_{i+1},\qquad k_i<k_{i+1}$$

whenever the indicated indices occur, define the **Jones normal-form word**

$$N(j,k):=(u_{j_1}u_{j_1-1}\cdots u_{k_1})(u_{j_2}u_{j_2-1}\cdots u_{k_2})\cdots(u_{j_r}u_{j_r-1}\cdots u_{k_r});$$

for $r=0$ it is the empty word $1$. Let $\mathcal N_n$ be the set of these formal words. Every generator monomial in $P_n(R,\delta)$ is equal either to $0$ or to $\delta^sN$ for some $s\ge0$ and $N\in\mathcal N_n$. The set $\mathcal N_n$ is in bijection with Dyck paths of semilength $n$; consequently it has $C_n$ elements and spans $P_n(R,\delta)$. This theorem asserts spanning and the count of the named candidates, not their linear independence.

For $R$, $\delta$, $n$, $t$ and $W_{n,t}(R,\delta)$ as in [[def-temperley-lieb-link-state-standard-modules]], the rule $x\cdot a=[x\circ a]$ defines a unital right $\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$-module structure on $W_{n,t}(R,\delta)$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit, $\delta\in R$, $n\ge1$, and let $t$ be allowed for $W_{n,t}(R,\delta)$. Include $\mathrm{TL}_{n-1}(R,\delta)$ into $\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$ by adding a rightmost vertical strand, and restrict the right action along this inclusion. Set $W_{m,s}=0$ when $s<0$, $s>m$, or $m-s$ is odd. Then there is a short exact sequence of right $\mathrm{TL}_{n-1}(R,\delta)$-modules

$$0\longrightarrow W_{n-1,t-1}\longrightarrow \operatorname{Res}^{TL_n}_{TL_{n-1}}W_{n,t}\longrightarrow W_{n-1,t+1}\longrightarrow0.$$

The sequence gives a two-step filtration; it is not asserted to split.

Let $q\in\mathbb C^\times$, $\delta=q+q^{-1}$, $n\ge0$, and $0\le p\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$. Put $t=n-2p$, and let $G_{n,p}$ be the Gram matrix of the link-state form on $W_{n,t}(\mathbb C,\delta)$ in its link-state basis. Set

$$d_{n,r}=\binom nr-\binom n{r-1},\qquad \binom n{-1}=0.$$

Then

$$\det G_{n,p}=\prod_{j=1}^{p}\left(\frac{[n-2p+1+j]_q}{[j]_q}\right)^{d_{n,p-j}}.$$

The empty product for $p=0$ is $1$. The right side is interpreted as its polynomial continuation in $\delta$ at parameter values where an individual displayed quotient has a removable zero-over-zero form.

Let $q\in\mathbb C^\times$. Define $\kappa=\operatorname{ord}(q^2)$ if $q^2$ has finite multiplicative order, and $\kappa=\infty$ otherwise. For integers $n\ge0$ and $p$ with $0\le p\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, set the defect label $t=n-2p$; here $p$ counts arcs and $t$ counts defects. The pair $(n,p)$ is **critical** at $q$ when $\kappa<\infty$ and $\kappa\mid(t+1)$, equivalently $q^{2(t+1)}=1$. If $\kappa=\infty$, no pair is critical. When $\kappa=1$ every allowed pair is critical.

For finite $\kappa\ge2$ and a noncritical pair, write uniquely
$$t+1=k\kappa+r,\qquad k\ge0,\quad 1\le r<\kappa.$$
Its reflection label across the next critical line is
$$p^\sharp=p+r-\kappa.$$
This reflected label is called present only when $p^\sharp\ge0$; it then automatically satisfies $p^\sharp\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$. If $p^\sharp<0$, there is no label in range on that side. A critical label is treated as a singleton under reflection. These are arithmetic label conventions; they do not by themselves assert radical, composition-factor, Hom-space, or projective-cover formulas.

The order $\kappa$ is kept separate from the recurrence quantum characteristic $\ell$ of [[def-temperley-lieb-quantum-integers-and-quantum-characteristic]]. For $q=\pm1$, $\kappa=1$ while the complex recurrence quantum characteristic is $\infty$.

derivations.claim: It suffices to perform computations for left modules: send a right module to the left module with $a\cdot v=v\cdot a^*$, where $*$ is diagram reflection. This is an exact equivalence preserving Hom direction, induction and restriction. Fix a square root of $q$ and put $g_i=q^{1/2}1-q^{-1/2}d_i$. Expanding with [F1] gives $g_i^{-1}=q^{-1/2}1-q^{1/2}d_i$ and $g_ig_{i+1}g_i=g_{i+1}g_ig_{i+1}$. Let $T_n:A_{n+1}\to A_n$ close the last top endpoint to the last bottom endpoint externally on the right, removing any resulting loop with factor $\delta$. This is an $A_n$-bimodule map by the matching rule. Define $M_n=g_n\cdots g_2g_1^2g_2\cdots g_n$ and $F_n=T_n(M_n)$; set $F_0=\delta$. Every summand of $M_n$ has an even total number of square-root factors, so $F_n$ has coefficients in $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$, independent of the chosen square root.

For clarity give a basis proof of the induction sequence. In left-module notation put $h_r=d_rd_{r+1}\cdots d_n$ for $1\le r\le n$, and $h_{n+1}=1$. A state $d$ is $r$-admissible when it has no adjacent arc at an index $i\ge r$. The tensors $h_r\otimes d$ with $d$ $r$-admissible, including all $1\otimes d$, span $A_{n+1}\otimes_{A_n}V_{n,p}$. First, a diagram word is a sum of $h_ru$ with $u\in A_n$: reverse a spanning Jones normal form from [F1]. Its initial ascending block is either $h_r$ or contains no $d_n$, and every later block lies in $A_n$. The surjection from the presented algebra to the diagram algebra is supplied by the local relations, so this spanning assertion applies to diagram words. Next, if $d$ has its largest adjacent arc at $s\ge r$, write $d=d_sf$. For $n\ge3$ this can be done without division: move the endpoint immediately outside that adjacent arc through the arc, so applying $d_s$ restores $d$ and creates no loop. If $s=1$ use site $3$; otherwise use site $s-1$. The outside site is either a defect or an endpoint of another arc, and reconnecting its former partner supplies the inverse state $f$. Now the relations give $h_r\otimes d=h_{s+2}\otimes d_r\cdots d_{s-1}d$. The latter state is $(s+2)$-admissible: the adjacent arc at $s$ has moved to $r$, all intervening endpoints shift by two, and the tail beyond $s+1$ still has no adjacent arc. Repetition, increasing $r$, proves spanning. At $n=1,2$ the same conclusion is checked on the at most two states, except $n=2,p=1,\delta=0$, when the needed factorization $d=d_1f$ fails.

The braid relations give $g_iM_n=M_ng_i$ for $i<n$. To see this directly, commute $g_i$ past all $g_j$ with $|j-i|>1$ in the descending and ascending strings; the remaining equality is $g_ig_{i+1}g_i=g_{i+1}g_ig_{i+1}$ on each side of the middle string. This proves the equality inductively in the length of the strings, starting with $g_1g_2g_1^2g_2=g_2g_1^2g_2g_1$. Bimodule linearity of $T_n$ gives $g_iF_n=F_ng_i$, hence $d_iF_n=F_nd_i$. Thus $F_n$ is central. Reversing the palindromic word $M_n$ and reflecting its closure leaves it unchanged, so $F_n^*=F_n$.

Compute $F_n$ on the state $z_p$ with adjacent arcs $(1,2),(3,4),\ldots,(2p-1,2p)$ and all remaining sites defects. At a cup, expansion of the two adjacent crossings uses the identities $d_ig_{i+1}g_i=-d_id_{i+1}$ and $g_ig_{i+1}d_i=-d_{i+1}d_i$; for example the first is $qd_i-d_id_{i+1}-\delta d_i+q^{-1}d_id_{i+1}d_i=-d_id_{i+1}$. The two minus signs on the two sides of each cup cancel. Thus each initial cup can be removed without changing the coefficient of $z_p$. For the $t=n-2p$ defect strands, expand the auxiliary strand successively from its first crossing. A smoothing connecting two defects vanishes in the standard quotient. There are two remaining continuations: following the auxiliary strand on its two sides gives respectively $q^t\delta-q^{t-1}=q^{t+1}$ and $q^{-t}\delta-q^{-t+1}=q^{-(t+1)}$. The factors arise by choosing the identity smoothing at each subsequent crossing until the final cap; that cap either closes a loop or chooses the second smoothing, giving the displayed two terms on each side. Hence the coefficient of $z_p$ is $f_{n,p}$. For generic $q$, [F3] makes the form nondegenerate. Capping $z$ against $y$ and then attaching $x$ gives the rank-one diagram operator $z\mapsto\phi(y,z)x$, because lower-propagating terms vanish. Thus every nonzero vector generates the standard, which is simple. Centrality now makes $F_n$ scalar on the entire standard: over $\mathbb C$ a central operator has an eigenvalue, whose nonzero eigenspace is the simple module. Since the action matrices and $f_{n,p}$ are Laurent polynomial in $q$, this scalar identity extends to every $q\ne0$.

On the submodule and quotient in [F2], $F_{n-1}$ acts by $f_{n-1,p}$ and $f_{n-1,p-1}$. Their difference is $-(q-q^{-1})(q^{n-2p+1}-q^{-(n-2p+1)})$. Under the noncritical and $q\ne\pm1$ hypotheses it is nonzero. The operator on the restriction satisfies $(F_{n-1}-f_{n-1,p})(F_{n-1}-f_{n-1,p-1})=0$, because each factor kills its respective subquotient. Its two spectral projections therefore give an invariant direct sum splitting the restriction sequence.

Append an adjacent arc at sites $n+1,n+2$ to $d$, obtaining $\bar d\in V_{n+2,p+1}$. The map $\Phi(u\otimes d)=u\bar d$ into $V_{n+2,p+1}\downarrow$ is balanced and $A_{n+1}$-linear: elements of $A_n$ act only on the first $n$ sites. Its image of $h_r\otimes d$ has its rightmost adjacent arc at $r$; deleting that arc recovers $d$. Conversely every $(n+2,p+1)$-state has a rightmost adjacent arc; delete it at position $r$, and the remaining state is $r$-admissible. These two operations are inverse, so the spanning tensors in step 1.2 map bijectively to the link-state basis. They are therefore a basis and $\Phi$ is an isomorphism, except in the stated exceptional case. Applying the restriction sequence [F2] to $V_{n+2,p+1}$ now gives the asserted induction sequence. Applying step 4.1 at rank $n+2$ splits it whenever $(n,p)$ is noncritical, since $n+2-2(p+1)+1=n-2p+1$.

Suppose $(n,p)$ is critical, $q
e\pm1$, and $z_p$ is as in step 3.1. In the induced basis the coefficient of $h_{2p+1}\otimes z_p$ in $F_{n+1}(1\otimes z_p)$ is $(-1)^n(\delta^2-4)
e0.$ Here is the local expansion computing it. First take $p=0$. To leave $h_1=d_1\cdots d_n$ after reduction, the first pair of crossings of the closed auxiliary strand has three contributing smoothings, with weights $-1,-1,\delta q^{-1}$; the fourth, of weight $q$, closes off the needed through path. This gives $-2+\delta q^{-1}$. At each of the next $n-1$ pairs exactly one continuation retains the required external matching, of weight $-1$: the other continuation either caps the auxiliary path prematurely or makes an additional bottom arc. At the final pair the corresponding three weights are $-1,-1,\delta q$, giving $-2+\delta q$. Their product is $(-1)^{n-1}(-2+\delta q^{-1})(-2+\delta q)=(-1)^n(\delta^2-4)$. The required exterior matching of $h_1$ has top pair $(1,2)$, bottom pair $(n,n+1)$, and through paths from top $j+2$ to bottom $j$ for $1\le j<n$. Follow the auxiliary strand subject to these connections: a premature cap at an intermediate row would create another exterior arc instead of the required through path, so its continuation is excluded. For $p>0$, remove the first $p$ cups using the two local identities in step 3.1, on both sides of the auxiliary path. This leaves the same computation on $n-2p$ sites; $n-2p>0$ by criticality and $\kappa\ge2$, and its parity equals that of $n$. The target basis tensor is $h_{2p+1}\otimes z_p=h_1\otimes z_p$, by successive $d_id_{i+1}d_i=d_i$ reductions. One may do the cup removal first for $\delta
e0$ by inserting $\delta^{-1}d_{2j-1}$ at each initial cup. The resulting coefficient identity extends to $\delta=0$: the induced basis reduction in step 1.2 uses no division, so its matrices, and this coefficient, are Laurent polynomials in $q$. Finally $\delta^2-4=(q-q^{-1})^2
e0$.

In the induction sequence at a critical $(n,p)$ the two standard constituents have the same eigenvalue $f=f_{n+1,p}=f_{n+1,p+1}$. The central endomorphism $F_{n+1}-f$ kills both constituents but is nonzero on the induction by step 6.1. Consequently it factors through the quotient $V_{n+1,p}$ into the submodule $V_{n+1,p+1}$, giving a nonzero map between these adjacent reflected standards. Explicitly, lift a quotient vector to the induction, apply $F_{n+1}-f$, and use the inverse of the submodule injection; the result is independent of the lift because this operator kills the submodule.

Every symmetric pair has the form $(n+j,p),(n+j,p+j)$ for a critical $(n,p)$ and $1\le j<\kappa$. For $j\ge2$, induction and restriction at the noncritical labels give $\operatorname{Hom}(V_{n+j,p},V_{n+j,p+j})\cong\operatorname{Hom}(V_{n+j-1,p}\uparrow,V_{n+j,p+j})\cong\operatorname{Hom}(V_{n+j-1,p},V_{n+j,p+j}\downarrow)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(V_{n+j-1,p},V_{n+j-1,p+j-1}).$ In the first and last isomorphisms the extra standard summand has a different $F$-eigenvalue: substitute $q^{2(n-2p+1)}=1$ in step 3.1, and equality would force $j=1$ or $j=\kappa$. Thus its Hom is zero. The middle adjunction is explicit: $f\mapsto(v\mapsto f(1\otimes v))$, with inverse $g\mapsto(a\otimes v\mapsto ag(v))$. This works also when an extraneous summand is out of range. Reducing $j$ to $1$ and applying step 7.1 proves nonvanishing for every reflected pair. Returning along step 1.1 gives all statements for the repository's right modules.

citations.quote:
Work over $\mathbb C$, with $q\ne0$, $\delta=q+q^{-1}$. Write $A_n=\mathrm{TL}_n(\mathbb C,\delta)$ and $V_{n,p}=W_{n,n-2p}(\mathbb C,\delta)$. There is a central, reflection-invariant element $F_n\in A_n$ acting on $V_{n,p}$ by
$$f_{n,p}=q^{n-2p+1}+q^{-(n-2p+1)}.$$
When $q\ne\pm1$ and $(n,p)$ is noncritical, restriction splits as $V_{n,p}\downarrow=V_{n-1,p}\oplus V_{n-1,p-1}$. Except at $(n,p,\delta)=(2,1,0)$, induction has a natural exact sequence
$$0\longrightarrow V_{n+1,p+1}\longrightarrow V_{n,p}\uparrow\longrightarrow V_{n+1,p}\longrightarrow0,$$
which splits when $(n,p)$ is noncritical. Here induction of a right module means $V\otimes_{A_n}A_{n+1}$.

If $\kappa=\operatorname{ord}(q^2)\ge2$ and $p<p'$ are a pair reflected in a single intervening critical line, meaning $0<p'-p<\kappa$ and $p=p'+r(n,p')-\kappa$, then
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{A_n}(V_{n,p},V_{n,p'})\ne0.$$
Out-of-range standard modules are zero. Statements about a splitting omit zero summands.

Let $q\in\mathbb C^\times$, $\delta=q+q^{-1}$, $n\ge0$, and $0\le p\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$. Put $t=n-2p$, and let $G_{n,p}$ be the Gram matrix of the link-state form on $W_{n,t}(\mathbb C,\delta)$ in its link-state basis. Set

$$d_{n,r}=\binom nr-\binom n{r-1},\qquad \binom n{-1}=0.$$

Then

$$\det G_{n,p}=\prod_{j=1}^{p}\left(\frac{[n-2p+1+j]_q}{[j]_q}\right)^{d_{n,p-j}}.$$

The empty product for $p=0$ is $1$. The right side is interpreted as its polynomial continuation in $\delta$ at parameter values where an individual displayed quotient has a removable zero-over-zero form.

Let $q\in\mathbb C^\times$, $\delta=q+q^{-1}$, $n\ge0$, and $0\le p\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$. Put $t=n-2p$, let $\kappa=\operatorname{ord}(q^2)$, and let $\phi_{n,t}$ be the link-state capping form on $W_{n,t}(\mathbb C,\delta)$. If $(n,p)$ is critical in the sense of [[def-temperley-lieb-complex-critical-labels-and-reflection]], then $\phi_{n,t}$ is nondegenerate and $W_{n,t}(\mathbb C,\delta)$ is simple.

Let $R$, $\delta$, $n$, $t$ and $W_{n,t}(R,\delta)$ be as in [[def-temperley-lieb-link-state-standard-modules]]. For link states $x,y$, let $x^*$ denote reflection across a horizontal line. The diagram $y\circ x^*:t\to t$ is either $\delta^c1_t$ for some $c\ge0$ or has fewer than $t$ propagating components. Define $\phi_{n,t}(x,y)=\delta^c$ in the first case and $0$ in the second, and extend $R$-bilinearly. Then $\phi_{n,t}$ is symmetric and satisfies

$$\phi_{n,t}(x\cdot a,y)=\phi_{n,t}(x,y\cdot a^*)$$

for all $x,y\in W_{n,t}(R,\delta)$ and $a\in\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$. Here $a^*$ is reflection across a horizontal line. The matrix of $\phi_{n,t}$ in the link-state basis is the Gram matrix obtained by reflecting and capping two link states, with one factor $\delta$ for each closed loop.

Let $n\ge0$ and let $t$ satisfy $0\le t\le n$ and $n-t$ even. Put $a=(n-t)/2$, the number of arcs in a link state, and use the convention $\binom{n}{a-1}=0$ when $a=0$. Then the link-state basis $T_{n,t}$ of $W_{n,t}(R,\delta)$ has cardinality

$$|T_{n,t}|=\binom{n}{a}-\binom{n}{a-1}.$$

In particular, $W_{n,t}$ is free of this rank over $R$, independently of $\delta$.

Let $q\in\mathbb C^\times$. Define $\kappa=\operatorname{ord}(q^2)$ if $q^2$ has finite multiplicative order, and $\kappa=\infty$ otherwise. For integers $n\ge0$ and $p$ with $0\le p\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, set the defect label $t=n-2p$; here $p$ counts arcs and $t$ counts defects. The pair $(n,p)$ is **critical** at $q$ when $\kappa<\infty$ and $\kappa\mid(t+1)$, equivalently $q^{2(t+1)}=1$. If $\kappa=\infty$, no pair is critical. When $\kappa=1$ every allowed pair is critical.

For finite $\kappa\ge2$ and a noncritical pair, write uniquely
$$t+1=k\kappa+r,\qquad k\ge0,\quad 1\le r<\kappa.$$
Its reflection label across the next critical line is
$$p^\sharp=p+r-\kappa.$$
This reflected label is called present only when $p^\sharp\ge0$; it then automatically satisfies $p^\sharp\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$. If $p^\sharp<0$, there is no label in range on that side. A critical label is treated as a singleton under reflection. These are arithmetic label conventions; they do not by themselves assert radical, composition-factor, Hom-space, or projective-cover formulas.

The order $\kappa$ is kept separate from the recurrence quantum characteristic $\ell$ of [[def-temperley-lieb-quantum-integers-and-quantum-characteristic]]. For $q=\pm1$, $\kappa=1$ while the complex recurrence quantum characteristic is $\infty$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit and $\delta\in R$. Define the quantum integers by

$$[0]_\delta=0,\qquad [1]_\delta=1,\qquad [r+1]_\delta=\delta[r]_\delta-[r-1]_\delta\quad(r\ge1).$$

The **quantum characteristic** of $(R,\delta)$ is the least positive integer $\ell$ with $[\ell]_\delta=0$, if one exists, and $\ell=\infty$ otherwise. No element of $R$ is inverted in this definition.

For $q\in\mathbb C^\times$ and $\delta=q+q^{-1}$, write $[r]_q=[r]_\delta$. If $q\ne\pm1$, this agrees with $(q^r-q^{-r})/(q-q^{-1})$; at $q=\pm1$ the recurrence gives $[r]_q=rq^{r-1}$. For complex-parameter classification, write $\kappa=\operatorname{ord}(q^2)$, with $\kappa=\infty$ when $q^2$ has infinite order. If $q\ne\pm1$, the quantum characteristic equals $\kappa$ when $\kappa<\infty$ and is $\infty$ otherwise. At $q=\pm1$, $\kappa=1$ but the complex quantum characteristic is $\infty$, because $[r]_q=rq^{r-1}\ne0$ for every positive $r$.

For a field $K$ of positive characteristic $p$, set $p(0)=1$ and, when $\ell<\infty$, set $p(i)=\ell p^{i-1}$ for $i\ge1$. In characteristic zero and finite $\ell$, the finite digit scale is $p(1)=\ell$; the separate characteristic-zero criterion below uses $a\ell-1$ for arbitrary positive integers $a$. If $\ell=\infty$, every finite index is already in the range $n<\ell$.

derivations.claim: First work at generic $q$. The rightmost-defect submodule has nondegenerate form by [F2], so its orthogonal complement is invariant and maps isomorphically to the restriction quotient. The smaller standards are simple by their rank-one diagram operators; an invariant form on such a standard is a scalar multiple of its nondegenerate standard form, because their associated maps into the dual differ by an endomorphism, and an endomorphism of a finite-dimensional complex simple module is scalar (take any eigenvalue). Subtracting the submodule projection from quotient basis lifts gives a unitriangular Gram splitting $G_{n,p}=U^{\mathsf T}(G_{n-1,p}\oplus\alpha_{n,p}G_{n-1,p-1})U$. Compute its scalar as follows. Group the link states into the four types: $n,n-1$ both defects; $n$ a defect and $n-1$ on an earlier arc; $(n-1,n)$ an arc; and $n$ on an arc ending earlier than $n-1$. Put $A=G_{n-2,p}$, $B=G_{n-2,p-1}$ and write the smaller-rank matrix as $G_{n-1,p}=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}A&AV_0\\V_0^{\mathsf T}A&V_0^{\mathsf T}AV_0+\alpha_{n-1,p}B\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. In the current off-diagonal Gram block the first column block is $(0,B)^{\mathsf T}$: types one and three have unmatched defects, while cutting the terminal arc in types two and three removes no closed component. The type-three diagonal block is $\delta B$, since the shared terminal arc closes one loop. If $(X,Y)^{\mathsf T}$ is the first column block of the projection coefficient matrix, multiplication by $G_{n-1,p}$ gives $AX+AV_0Y=0$ and $V_0^{\mathsf T}AX+(V_0^{\mathsf T}AV_0+\alpha_{n-1,p}B)Y=B$. Thus $X=-V_0Y$ and $Y=\alpha_{n-1,p}^{-1}I$. Its quadratic contribution is $\alpha_{n-1,p}^{-1}B$ after the four $V_0^{\mathsf T}AV_0$ terms cancel with coefficients $1-1-1+1$. Comparing the type-three block gives $\alpha_{n,p}=\delta-\alpha_{n-1,p}^{-1}$. At $n=2p$, deleting the terminal site closes exactly one additional component, so $G_{2p,p}=\delta G_{2p-1,p-1}$ and $\alpha_{2p,p}=\delta$. The recurrence solves to $\alpha_{n,p}=[n-2p+2]_q/[n-2p+1]_q$ by the quantum-integer recurrence. If the $A$ block is empty it is omitted; the same cancellation still holds. Now at a noncritical root, the two eigenvalues used for [F1] differ by $-(q-q^{-1})(q^{n-2p+1}-q^{-(n-2p+1)})\ne0$. The spectral projector onto the rightmost-defect summand is $(F_{n-1}-f_{n-1,p-1})/(f_{n-1,p}-f_{n-1,p-1})$. Its entries are rational functions regular at the root; subtracting this projection from each standard quotient lift gives a unitriangular splitting matrix $U$, also regular there. Since $F_{n-1}^*=F_{n-1}$ and the eigenvalues differ, the two summands are orthogonal. For generic $q$ this is exactly the orthogonal splitting just computed, since the submodule form is nondegenerate and its orthogonal complement is unique. Thus this Gram matrix identity is an identity of rational matrices regular at every noncritical root, and specializes there. This continuity argument applies to the entire matrix identity, rather than inferring a rank from a specialized determinant. If $n=2p$, there is only the quotient summand and direct capping gives $G_{2p,p}=\delta G_{2p-1,p-1}$, the same formula with $\alpha=[2]/[1]=\delta$.

Since $\kappa\ge2$, $q\ne\pm1$; hence $[a]_q=0$ precisely when $\kappa\mid a$. At a noncritical label the denominator of $\alpha$ is nonzero and its numerator vanishes precisely when $r=\kappa-1$. The kernel dimension of the specialized block form in step 1.1 is therefore $\dim R_{n-1,p}+\dim V_{n-1,p-1}$ in that case, and $\dim R_{n-1,p}+\dim R_{n-1,p-1}$ otherwise. Critical labels give zero by [F3]; the all-defect form is $(1)$, giving $R_{n,0}=0$. For $n\ge1$, subtraction from [F4] gives the companion recursion, with initial $\dim L_{0,0}=1$: $\dim L_{n,p}=\dim V_{n,p}$ at critical labels; at noncritical labels it is $\dim L_{n-1,p}$ if $r=\kappa-1$, and $\dim L_{n-1,p}+\dim L_{n-1,p-1}$ otherwise.

Prove the reflected-dimension formula by induction on $n$, with out-of-range labels assigned dimension zero. Write $a=p+r-\kappa$. If $r\notin\{1,\kappa-1\}$, neither predecessor is critical. Their reflection indices are respectively $a-1$ and $a$, so induction and step 2.1 give $\dim R_{n,p}=\dim L_{n-1,a-1}+\dim L_{n-1,a}$. The reflected label $a$ has remainder $\kappa-r$, which is also neither $1$ nor $\kappa-1$; its companion recursion gives exactly $\dim L_{n,a}$.

When $\kappa=2$, every noncritical label has $r=1=\kappa-1$ and both predecessors are critical. The radical recursion gives $\dim R_{n,p}=\dim V_{n-1,p-1}=\dim L_{n-1,p-1}$. Since $a=p-1$ and the companion recursion at $(n,a)$ also has remainder $1$, this is $\dim L_{n,a}$. The same formula holds for $n=2p$: it gives $\dim R_{2p,p}=\dim V_{2p-1,p-1}=\dim V_{2p,p}$, as required by the identically zero form.

If $r=\kappa-1$ and $\kappa>2$, the predecessor $(n-1,p-1)$ is critical, while $(n-1,p)$ has reflected index $a-1$. Consequently $\dim R_{n,p}=\dim L_{n-1,a-1}+\dim V_{n-1,p-1}$. Here $a=p-1$, and criticality gives $V_{n-1,p-1}=L_{n-1,a}$. The companion recursion at $(n,a)$ has remainder $1\ne\kappa-1$, so this sum is $\dim L_{n,a}$. If $r=1$ and $\kappa>2$, $(n-1,p)$ is critical and its radical is zero; the reflection of $(n-1,p-1)$ has index $a$. Thus $\dim R_{n,p}=\dim L_{n-1,a}$. The reflected label at rank $n$ has remainder $\kappa-1$, whose companion recursion is precisely $\dim L_{n,a}=\dim L_{n-1,a}$.

The initial $p=0$ case has $a<0$ and zero radical. All predecessor terms whose indices leave the allowed range are zero. In particular the recursions in the preceding cases give zero when $a<0$; when $a=0$ they use the initial all-defect dimension $1$. These boundary rules also cover $n=0,1$. The induction establishes the stated formula for present reflected labels and the zero radical for absent labels.

citations.quote: Let $F$ be a field, $\delta\in F$, and $n\ge0$. Put $D_{n,t}=W_{n,t}(F,\delta)/\operatorname{rad}(\phi_{n,t})$ for each allowed $t$. Then the nonzero $D_{n,t}$ are absolutely simple and form a complete set of pairwise nonisomorphic simple right $\mathrm{TL}_n(F,\delta)$-modules. Moreover, $D_{n,t}\ne0$ exactly when $\phi_{n,t}$ is not identically zero; in that case $\operatorname{rad}(\phi_{n,t})$ is the unique maximal proper submodule and $D_{n,t}$ is the simple head of $W_{n,t}$. If $\phi_{n,t}$ is identically zero, then $D_{n,t}=0$, but no conclusion about the actual head of $W_{n,t}$ follows.

Put $V_{n,p}=W_{n,n-2p}(\mathbb C,q+q^{-1})$, $R_{n,p}=\operatorname{rad}\phi_{n,n-2p}$ and $L_{n,p}=V_{n,p}/R_{n,p}$, allowing $L_{2p,p}=0$ when $\delta=0$. Let $\kappa=\operatorname{ord}(q^2)\ge2$. For a noncritical label write $n-2p+1=k\kappa+r$ with $1\le r<\kappa$. Then

$$\dim R_{n,p}=\begin{cases}\dim R_{n-1,p}+\dim V_{n-1,p-1},&r=\kappa-1,\\\dim R_{n-1,p}+\dim R_{n-1,p-1},&r\ne\kappa-1.\end{cases}$$

Put $t=n-2p$, let $\kappa=\operatorname{ord}(q^2)$, and let $\phi_{n,t}$ be the link-state capping form on $W_{n,t}(\mathbb C,\delta)$. derivations.claim: The form is nonzero unless $\delta=0$ and the positive-rank defect number is zero. Indeed, when $\delta\ne0$ a state's pairing with itself is $\delta^p\ne0$. Their overlay on sites $1,\ldots,2p+1$ is one open alternating path, with no cycle, and all remaining defect paths match. Thus $\phi(x,y)=1$. If $p=0$ the form is $(1)$. First observe the rank-one identity: form the algebra diagram whose two halves are $x,y$. Stacking $z$ against its $y$ half gives $\phi(y,z)$ times the identity on the defect strands; if fewer strands propagate, it is zero in the standard quotient. Therefore this diagram sends $z$ to $\phi(y,z)x$, by exactly the matching rule in [F5]. More strongly, any submodule not contained in the form radical is the entire standard. If $z$ lies outside the radical, choose $y$ with $\phi(y,z)=1$. For any vector $x$, the diagram with halves $x,y$ sends $z$ to $x$ by [F5]; hence $z$ generates the standard. Its image also lies in $R_{n,p}$: otherwise step 2.1 makes $f$ surjective, and its inverse isomorphism $V_{n,p}\to V_{n,a}/\ker f$ contradicts the quotient-vanishing assertion in step 2.1. The source is never the zero-form exceptional label, since $a<p$. If the target is the exceptional label, its simplicity in [F4] instead gives $\operatorname{im}f=V_{n,p}=R_{n,p}$ directly. Thus in every case $\ker f\subseteq R_{n,a}$ and $\operatorname{im}f\subseteq R_{n,p}$.

Rank-nullity and [F3] now force equality in both inclusions: $\dim V_{n,a}=\dim\ker f+\dim\operatorname{im}f\le\dim R_{n,a}+\dim R_{n,p}=\dim R_{n,a}+\dim L_{n,a}=\dim V_{n,a}$. It has exactly the two displayed simple factors. The critical $\kappa=1$ branch is [F4]. If $\kappa=\infty$, no quantum integer in the determinant vanishes, so the determinant and hence the form are nondegenerate; this is [F6]. Exhaustion and distinction of the nonzero heads are [F1].

At $\delta=0$ and $n=2p>0$, $\kappa=2$ and the reflected arc label is $p-1$. Step 1.1 identifies the form radical as all of $V_{2p,p}$, while step 4.1 identifies it with $L_{2p,p-1}$. This agrees with the separately proved actual simplicity [F4]; its zero form quotient introduces no extra simple label. The remaining standards have nonzero forms and hence the complete simple labels are $0,\ldots,p-1$. Finally, each noncritical standard shares factors only with its adjacent reflection neighbors by step 4.1, and every present neighbor occurs. Taking the equivalence generated by these edges gives precisely the stated reflection chains. A critical head occurs only in its own simple standard, giving singleton classes.

derivations.claim: Stacking a state $z$ against the diagram with halves $y,x$ caps $z$ with $y$, giving $z\cdot C_{y,x}=\phi(y,z)x$; when propagation drops, both sides vanish in the standard quotient. This proves every diagonal dimension is one.

It remains to include $Z=V_{2m,m}$ at $\delta=0$. Here $Z\cong L_{2m,m-1}$ is simple by [F1]. For a nonexceptional source $V_{2m,p}$, a map to $Z$ has simple image; if nonzero it is a simple quotient of the source, hence its head $L_{2m,p}$. Distinctness of the labels forces $p=m-1$, in which case [F2] supplies a map and [F4] gives uniqueness. This is exactly the adjacent-reflection case.

Suppose both source and target have nonzero forms and $p>p'$. The rank-one operators for the source have $n-2p<n-2p'$ propagating strands and kill the target. Choosing $y,z$ as in step 1.1, a proposed homomorphism $h$ therefore satisfies $h(x)=h(z\cdot C_{y,x})=h(z)\cdot C_{y,x}=0$. Hence the Hom space is zero.

Suppose both forms are nonzero and $p<p'$. A nonzero map cannot be surjective: its inverse quotient isomorphism would contradict step 2.1, whose proof also applies to quotients of the target. Thus its image lies in the simple radical $R_{n,p'}$. The kernel is a proper submodule of the source and hence is $0$ or $R_{n,p}$. If it is zero, the source is simple because it embeds into the simple radical. In either case the image is isomorphic to the source head $L_{n,p}$. By [F1] and distinction of simple labels this is possible exactly when $p$ is the adjacent reflected label of $p'$. Such a map exists by [F2]; it factors as the head quotient followed by an isomorphism $L_{n,p}\cong R_{n,p'}$ and the radical inclusion. Schur's lemma makes this factorization unique up to scalar, so its Hom space has dimension one and the stated kernel and image. If the target radical is zero there is no such map.

A nonzero map from $Z$ to $V_{2m,p'}$, $p'<m$, is injective. If its image is the radical, [F1] makes it $L_{2m,p'-1}$; this cannot equal $L_{2m,m-1}$ because $p'-1<m-1$. derivations.claim: Fix a nonzero head $L=L_{n,p}$ and its finite-dimensional projective cover $\pi:P\to L$ from [F3]. Since $L$ is cyclic, choose a surjection $\alpha:A_n\to L$. Projectivity of $P$ and of the finite free module $A_n$ gives maps $s:P\to A_n$ and $t:A_n\to P$ with $\alpha s=\pi$ and $\pi t=\alpha$. Then $\pi ts=\pi$. Consequently $P=ts(P)+\ker\pi$; superfluity gives $ts(P)=P$, so $ts$ is invertible by finite dimensionality. Replacing $s$ by $s(ts)^{-1}$ makes $ts=1$. Thus $P$ is a direct summand $eA_n$ of the right regular module for an idempotent $e$ (a right-module endomorphism of $A_n$ is left multiplication by its value at $1$). The cover is indecomposable: a nonzero decomposition would give a proper summand surjecting onto $L$, contrary to the superfluous kernel.

If $S$ is any simple right module and $h:P\to S$ is nonzero, then its kernel is maximal. Superfluity of $\ker\pi$ implies $\ker\pi\subseteq\ker h$: otherwise their sum is $P$ and the superfluity condition would force $\ker h=P$. Thus $h$ factors through $L$. On a finite-dimensional complex simple module an endomorphism $u$ has an eigenvalue $\lambda$; since $u-\lambda1$ has a nonzero kernel, [F5] makes it zero. Thus its endomorphism space is $\mathbb C$. By [F1], $\dim\operatorname{Hom}_{A_n}(eA_n,S)$ is $1$ for $S=L$ and $0$ otherwise. Evaluation at $e$ identifies this Hom space with $Se$: the inverse sends $v\in Se$ to the map $ea\mapsto va$. Hence $\dim Se$ has those same values. This also proves any finite-dimensional projective module surjecting onto $L$ contains $P$ as a summand, by repeating step 1.1 with that module in place of $A_n$. Finally every indecomposable projective has a simple quotient, hence is the cover of that quotient by this summand assertion.

Left multiplication by $e$ is an exact functor on left modules: for an exact sequence, a lift of $ey$ can be replaced by $e$ times that lift. The cellular basis itself identifies each ideal layer in [F2] with $U_s\otimes V_{n,s}$: map its basis tensor $x\otimes y$ to the class of $C^t_{x,y}$. Right multiplication acts only on $y$ by the cellular triangular rule, and left multiplication acts only on $x$ by reflecting that rule; this proves the bimodule identification, including the zero-form layers. Apply the exact functor to this ideal filtration. The resulting filtration of $eA_n=P$ has layer $(eU_s)\otimes V_{n,s}$, a direct sum of $\dim eU_s$ copies of $V_{n,s}$. Every simple constituent of $U_s$ is the reflected left version of a simple constituent of $V_{n,s}$, because reflection is an exact equivalence. By the invariant quotient forms in [F1], that reflected simple is the ordinary left dual of the corresponding right simple $S$. Its $e$-image has dimension $\dim Se$, since $e$ acts by the transpose operator on the dual. Exactness and step 2.1 therefore give $\dim eU_s=[V_{n,s}:L_{n,p}]$. We have proved, without a semisimplicity or quasiheredity assumption, a standard filtration $[P_{n,p}:V_{n,s}]=[V_{n,s}:L_{n,p}].$ In particular its layer order is increasing defect number, equivalently decreasing arc count.

At a critical label, [F1] says the only standard containing $L_{n,p}$ is $V_{n,p}$, once. Step 3.1 gives $P_{n,p}\cong V_{n,p}$. The same argument applies to every label at $\kappa=1,\infty$. At a finite-order noncritical nonzero head, the standards containing it are $V_{n,p}$ and, when present, its neighbor on the lower-defect side, $V_{n,b}$ with $b=p+r$. This follows by solving the adjacent-reflection relation in [F1] in the reverse direction. If $k=0$, $n-2b+1=-r<0$ and $b$ is absent. If $k>0$, $n-2b=k\kappa-r-1\ge0$ and it is present. Each occurrence has multiplicity one. At $\kappa=2$, even rank, the possible $b=n/2$ is included because the zero-form standard is the actual simple $L_{n,n/2-1}$ by [F1]. Thus step 3.1 gives either $P_{n,p}=V_{n,p}$ or exactly the asserted two-standard filtration. Since $b>p$, its $V_{n,b}$ layer is a submodule and its $V_{n,p}$ layer the quotient, yielding the exact sequence. It is nonsplit: both standards are nonzero, whereas the cover in step 1.1 is indecomposable.

For $k>0$, the starting label $(n-r,p)$ has defect number $k\kappa-1$ and is critical; its standard is projective by step 4.1. Induction preserves projectivity: the adjunction in [F4] identifies maps from an induced module with maps from the original module into a restriction, and restriction preserves surjections, so the defining lifting property is preserved. The $r$-fold induced module $Q$ is therefore projective. Repeatedly applying the standard induction sequences gives a filtration of $Q$ whose layers are quotients of the standards $V_{n,p+j}$, $0\le j\le r$, with multiplicities at most $\binom rj$. To justify this even though induction is only right exact, induct the existing filtration: the images of its submodules still form a filtration, and each new layer is a quotient of the induction of the old layer; the two-term sequence in [F4] refines these layers. No left-exactness is assumed. The exceptional induction input $(2,1,0)$ is never encountered: every intermediate defect is at least $k\kappa-1-(r-1)>0$.

On the standard indexed by $p+j$ the central eigenvalue is $q^{k\kappa+r-2j}+q^{-(k\kappa+r-2j)}$. It equals $f_{n,p}$ exactly when $j\equiv0$ or $j\equiv r\pmod\kappa$: use $x+x^{-1}=y+y^{-1}$ if and only if $(x-y)(x-y^{-1})=0$, and $q^{2k\kappa}=1$. Since $0\le j\le r<\kappa$, only $j=0,r$ qualify. Generalized eigenspaces of a central operator are submodules; the associated polynomial spectral projection is exact on finite-dimensional modules, as is seen by applying the same projection to a lift. Thus the $f_{n,p}$-space $Q_f$ is projective and step 5.1 bounds its dimension by $\dim V_{n,p}+\dim V_{n,p+r}$. Successive standard quotient maps give a surjection $Q\to V_{n,p}\to L_{n,p}$; its restriction to $Q_f$ remains onto, because the other generalized eigenspaces have distinct eigenvalues. Step 2.1 makes $P_{n,p}$ a direct summand of $Q_f$. Step 4.1 already gives $\dim P_{n,p}=\dim V_{n,p}+\dim V_{n,p+r}$, so the bound is saturated and $Q_f\cong P_{n,p}$, proving the stated realization.

At $\delta=0$, $\kappa=2$. Odd ranks have only critical labels and are covered by step 4.1. At rank $2m$, the simple labels are $0\le p<m$ by [F1]; each has $r=1$ and $k>0$. The repeated-induction realization in step 6.1 therefore has just one induction, from the odd-rank critical standard $V_{2m-1,p}$. Its two standard constituents both have eigenvalue $0$, so the entire induction is the selected generalized eigenspace. This proves the final displayed formulas and excludes a cover for the zero quotient label. At rank zero the algebra is $\mathbb C$, whose single simple regular module is projective. All covers and all exceptional cases have now been included.

citations.quote:
Fix an integer $\ell\ge3$ and set $q=e^{\pi i/\ell}$, so the multiplicative order of $q^2$ is $\ell$. Use the divided-power integral form of [[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]] from [[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]], specialized by $v\mapsto q$ to $\mathbb C$. In type $A_1$, write $K=K_h$ and $E,F$ for the rank-one generators. The convention is

$$KEK^{-1}=q^2E,\qquad KFK^{-1}=q^{-2}F,\qquad [E,F]=\frac{K-K^{-1}}{q-q^{-1}},$$

$$\Delta(K)=K\otimes K,\qquad \Delta(E)=E\otimes K+1\otimes E,\qquad \Delta(F)=F\otimes1+K^{-1}\otimes F.$$

This is the Sawin coproduct, rather than the inverse-$K$ coproduct in [[thm-the-drinfeld-jimbo-formulas-define-a-hopf-algebra]]. Its counit is $\varepsilon(K)=1$, $\varepsilon(E)=\varepsilon(F)=0$ and its antipode is $S(E)=-EK^{-1}$, $S(F)=-KF$, $S(K)=K^{-1}$. The exact integral transport is from the library algebra with opposite coproduct, by $E_{\rm target}=KE_{\rm lib}$, $F_{\rm target}=F_{\rm lib}K^{-1}$ and $K_{\rm target}=K_{\rm lib}$. Substituting these generators gives the displayed coproduct and unchanged mixed relation. On divided powers the formulas are $E_{\rm target}^{(r)}=v^{-r(r-1)}K^rE_{\rm lib}^{(r)}$ and $F_{\rm target}^{(r)}=v^{r(r-1)}F_{\rm lib}^{(r)}K^{-r}$; the inverse formulas also have Laurent-monomial coefficients, so the integral lattice and toral generators are preserved.

The Lusztig specialization includes all divided powers $E^{(r)},F^{(r)}$ and the toral quantum binomials; this is the divided-power form, not the small quantum group. A finite-dimensional module is **type 1** when it carries its integral-weight grading $M=\bigoplus_{m\in\mathbb Z}M_m$ with $K|_{M_m}=q^m$, the full toral character $T_{c,t}|_{M_m}=\begin{bmatrix}m+c\\t\end{bmatrix}_q I$ for every $c\in\mathbb Z$ and $t\ge0$, and $E^{(r)}M_m\subseteq M_{m+2r}$, $F^{(r)}M_m\subseteq M_{m-2r}$. The binomial is its Laurent-polynomial specialization, including negative upper indices. The grading is part of the data and is not collapsed when distinct weights have the same $K$ eigenvalue. Every module intertwiner preserves it: for $m<n$, $T_{-m,n-m}$ has eigenvalues $0$ and $1$ on weights $m$ and $n$.

For $a\ge0$, the Weyl module $\Delta(a)$ has basis $v_0,\ldots,v_a$ and actions

$$Kv_j=q^{a-2j}v_j,\qquad E^{(r)}v_j=\begin{bmatrix}a-j+r\\r\end{bmatrix}_qv_{j-r},\qquad F^{(r)}v_j=\begin{bmatrix}j+r\\r\end{bmatrix}_qv_{j+r},$$

where the Gaussian binomials are the Laurent-polynomial specializations of [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]], and $v_j=0$ outside $0\le j\le a$. Its dual is the dual Weyl module $\nabla(a)=\Delta(a)^\vee$. A **Weyl filtration** (respectively dual-Weyl filtration) is a finite submodule filtration whose successive quotients are modules $\Delta(a)$ (respectively $\nabla(a)$). A **tilting module** is a module with both filtrations.

Take $s=e^{\pi i/(2\ell)}$, so $s^2=q$. The ribbon category is the full weight-lattice extension $\mathcal U_s^\dagger(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ of this Lusztig form, not its root-lattice restriction. Its toral factor is the completed function algebra on the weight lattice $P=\mathbb Z\omega$, acting on each weight space by its weight character. Before specialization, the rank-one universal $R$-matrix is the Sawin weight-lattice expression

$R=D\sum_{r\ge0}q^{r(r+1)/2}(1-q^{-2})^r[r]_q!E^{(r)}\otimes F^{(r)},\qquad D|_{M_m\otimes N_n}=s^{mn}.$

interpreted in the completed tensor product; at the root it means the image of the integral completed form, not termwise division by a vanishing $[r]_q!$. In ordinary powers the coefficient is $q^{r(r-1)/2}(q-q^{-1})^r/[r]_q!$; changing to two divided powers multiplies that coefficient by $([r]_q!)^2$. Thus the displayed divided-power coefficient is Laurent integral and vanishes for $r\ge\ell$ after specialization. The toral factor is the weight pairing, fixed explicitly by $D$ above. The pivotal map is $j_M(x)(\varphi)=\varphi(Kx)$ and the twist is $\theta=u^{-1}j$ for the Drinfeld map $u$. The object class of this page is the full subcategory of finite-dimensional integrable type-1 tilting modules for this weight-lattice ribbon extension. No assertion about semisimplicity or the trace radical is part of this definition.

Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum for a quantum
group with $a_{ii}=2$ for all $i$
([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]), let
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$ be its Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra
([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]) with $q_i=q^{d_i}$ and
$K_i=K_{d_ih_i}$, and set

$$A:=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]\ \subseteq\ \mathbb Q(q),$$

the image of the Laurent polynomial ring $\Lambda_1=\mathbb Z[t]_{S}$ of
[[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]] under the unital ring homomorphism sending
$t$ to the indeterminate $q$; this homomorphism is injective and $A$ is a
subring of $\mathbb Q(q)$ (Verification, step 1.1). We work over this
commutative domain $A$ inside the field $\mathbb Q(q)$.

For $i\in I$, $c\in\mathbb Z$ and $t\ge0$ define the **toral quantum binomial**

$$T_{i,c,t}:=\begin{bmatrix}K_i;c\\ t\end{bmatrix}:=\prod_{s=1}^{t}\frac{K_iq_i^{\,c-s+1}-K_i^{-1}q_i^{\,-c+s-1}}{q_i^{\,s}-q_i^{\,-s}}\in U_q(\mathfrak g),$$

the empty product being $T_{i,c,0}:=1$. Each factor is defined in
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$ because $q_i^{\,s}-q_i^{\,-s}\ne0$ for $s\ge1$
([[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]), so
$T_{i,c,t}$ is a polynomial in $K_i^{\pm1}$ with coefficients in $\mathbb Q(q)$;
in particular all $T_{i,c,t}$ commute with the $K_h$ and with one another
(Verification, step 2.1).

The **Lusztig divided-power integral form** is the $A$-subalgebra

$$U_A:=\bigl\langle E_i^{(r)},\ F_i^{(r)},\ K_h^{\pm1},\ T_{i,c,t}\ \colon\ i\in I,\ r,t\ge0,\ c\in\mathbb Z,\ h\in P^{\vee}\bigr\rangle\ \subseteq\ U_q(\mathfrak g),$$

where $x^{(r)}=x^r/[r]_i!$ are the divided powers of
[[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]. Write $U_A^\pm$
for the $A$-subalgebras generated by the $E_i^{(r)}$ and by the $F_i^{(r)}$,
and $U_A^0$ for the one generated by the $K_h^{\pm1}$ and the $T_{i,c,t}$.

Then:

(i) $U_A$ contains $E_i=E_i^{(1)}$, $F_i=F_i^{(1)}$ and all $K_h$;

(ii) $U_A$ is a root-graded $A$-subalgebra of the root-graded
$\mathbb Q(q)$-algebra $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ ([[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]):
with $U_A[\beta]:=U_A\cap U_q(\mathfrak g)[\beta]$ one has
$U_A=\bigoplus_{\beta\in Q}U_A[\beta]$, each $U_A[\beta]$ is an $A$-submodule,
and $U_A^\pm,U_A^0$ are graded in the same way;

(iii) $U_A\otimes_A\mathbb Q(q)\cong U_q(\mathfrak g)$ canonically, i.e. the
$\mathbb Q(q)$-span of $U_A$ is all of $U_q(\mathfrak g)$.

The shifted binomials $T_{i,c,t}$ with $c\ne0$ are included because the
divided-power reordering identity of
[[lem-divided-power-and-toral-quantum-binomial-reordering-identities]] has
coefficients $T_{i,2t-a-b,t}$ with a nonconstant index; the specializations at
$q=1$ of these elements are computed in
[[lem-q-one-toral-specialization-identifies-the-classical-cartan-generators]],
and the integral triangular decomposition and the specialization are treated
only after this definition.

No freeness of $U_A$ or of its parts over $A$, no independence of the listed
generators, and no triangularity of the products of the three parts is asserted
here. In particular $A$ is not a principal ideal domain (Verification, step
7.1), so no torsion-free-to-free inference over $A$ is permitted anywhere on
this page.

Fix a symmetrizable Cartan datum $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$, an index $i\in I$, and put $q_i=q^{d_i}$. Let $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ be the Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra and let $A_i$ be the subalgebra generated by $E_i,F_i,K_i^{\pm1}$ ([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]], [[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]); write $x^{(m)}:=x^m/[m]_i!$ for the divided powers of [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]].

(i) The assignment $e\mapsto E_i$, $f\mapsto F_i$, $k\mapsto K_i$, $k^{-1}\mapsto K_i^{-1}$ defines an algebra isomorphism from the standard rank-one algebra $\mathbb A$ over $\mathbb Q(q)$, presented by $e,f,k^{\pm1}$ with $kek^{-1}=q_i^2e$, $kfk^{-1}=q_i^{-2}f$ and $[e,f]=(k-k^{-1})/(q_i-q_i^{-1})$ onto $A_i$; the images of the monomials $F_i^aK_i^mE_i^b$ ($a,b\ge0$, $m\in\mathbb Z$) are linearly independent in $U_q(\mathfrak g)$, being images of the PBW monomials of the triangular decomposition ([[thm-triangular-decomposition-of-a-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]).

(ii) For all $a,b\ge0$, $K_iE_i^{(a)}K_i^{-1}=q_i^{2a}E_i^{(a)}$ and $K_iF_i^{(b)}K_i^{-1}=q_i^{-2b}F_i^{(b)}$, and for $b\ge1$ the divided powers satisfy the exact commutation formula
$$E_iF_i^{(b)}=F_i^{(b)}E_i+\frac{F_i^{(b-1)}}{q_i^{b}-q_i^{-b}}\sum_{s=0}^{b-1}\bigl(q_i^{-2s}K_i-q_i^{2s}K_i^{-1}\bigr);$$
iterating it computes $E_i^{(a)}F_i^{(b)}$ as a finite sum of monomials $F_i^{(b-t)}K_i^{m}E_i^{(a-t)}$ ($0\le t\le\min(a,b)$) with coefficients in $\mathbb Q(q)$.

(iii) For every $N\ge0$ there is a simple $A_i$-module $L_i(N)$ of dimension $N+1$: it is the quotient of the cyclic module $\widetilde M(N):=A_i/\bigl(A_iE_i+A_i(K_i-q_i^N)\bigr)$ by the submodule generated by $F_i^{(N+1)}w_N$, where $w_N$ is the image of $1$, with basis the images $v_t$ of $F_i^{(t)}w_N$, $0\le t\le N$, on which $K_iv_t=q_i^{N-2t}v_t$, $F_iv_t=[t+1]_iv_{t+1}$ and $E_iv_t=[N-t+1]_iv_{t-1}$ (with $v_{-1}=v_{N+1}=0$); $L_i(N)$ is the unique simple $A_i$-module generated by a vector $v\ne0$ with $E_iv=0$, $K_iv=q_i^Nv$ and $F_i^{N+1}v=0$.

Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum for a quantum group ([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]) and put $q_i=q^{d_i}$. For $m\in\mathbb N$, define the **$q_i$-integer**

$$[m]_i:=\frac{q_i^m-q_i^{-m}}{q_i-q_i^{-1}},\qquad [0]_i:=0,$$

and the **$q_i$-factorial**

$$[m]_i!:=\prod_{k=1}^m[k]_i,\qquad [0]_i!:=1.$$

For $0\le r\le m$, define the **Gaussian binomial** $\binom{m}{r}_i:=[m]_i!/([r]_i![m-r]_i!)$, and set it to $0$ when $r<0$ or $r>m$. In the published one-parameter convention, write $\binom{m}{r}_t:=\binom{m}{r,m-r}_t$ for the two-part $q$-multinomial coefficient of [[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]].

For an element $x$ of a unital $\mathbb Q(q)$-algebra and $m\ge0$, define its **divided power at $q_i$** by $x^{(m)}:=x^m/[m]_i!$, so $x^{(0)}=1$ and $x^{(1)}=x$.

The symmetric convention and the published asymmetric convention are related, for $m\ge0$ and $0\le r\le m$, by

$$[m]_i=q_i^{-(m-1)}[m]_{q_i^2},\qquad \binom{m}{r}_i=q_i^{-r(m-r)}\binom{m}{r}_{q_i^2}.$$

In particular $[m]_i$ is invariant under $q_i\mapsto q_i^{-1}$. These quantities depend on the symmetrizer only through $q_i=q^{d_i}$.

Fix a symmetrizable Cartan datum and $i\in I$, and use the conventions of [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]. Write $C_{m,r}:=\binom{m}{r}_i$, with $C_{m,r}=0$ when $r<0$ or $r>m$.

(i) **Pascal recurrences.** For $m\ge1$ and every integer $r$,

$$C_{m,r}=q_i^{-r}C_{m-1,r}+q_i^{m-r}C_{m-1,r-1}=q_i^rC_{m-1,r}+q_i^{r-m}C_{m-1,r-1}.$$

(ii) **Symmetry.** For $0\le r\le m$, $C_{m,r}=C_{m,m-r}$.

(iii) **Gauss product formula.** For every $N\ge0$, in the polynomial ring $\mathbb Q(q)[z]$,

$$\prod_{j=0}^{N-1}(1+q_i^{2j}z)=\sum_{r=0}^{N}q_i^{r(N-1)}C_{N,r}z^r.$$

Consequently, for $N\ge1$,

$$\sum_{r=0}^{N}(-1)^rq_i^{r(N-1)}C_{N,r}=0.$$

(iv) **Integrality.** For $0\le r\le m$,

$$C_{m,r}\in q_i^{-r(m-r)}\mathbb Z[q_i^2]\subseteq\mathbb Z[q_i^{\pm1}].$$

Thus every Gaussian quotient is a Laurent polynomial in $q_i$ with integer coefficients, and the Pascal recurrences hold in that Laurent polynomial ring.

derivations.claim: The generic string lattice is stable under every divided power by [F2,F3], and $T_{c,t}v_j=\begin{bmatrix}a-2j+c\\t\end{bmatrix}_qv_j$ by the toral product. Hence it specializes to the stated full-weight module. More generally, if a full-weight module is supported on $[-a,a]$ and $w$ has weight $a$, the assignment $v_j\mapsto F^{(j)}w$ defines its unique map from $\Delta(a)$. Indeed the support kills every $E^{(r)}w$ for $r>0$ and every $F^{(j)}w$ for $j>a$. Divided-power straightening gives $E^{(r)}F^{(j)}w=\begin{bmatrix}a-j+r\\r\end{bmatrix}_qF^{(j-r)}w$, while $F^{(r)}F^{(j)}=\begin{bmatrix}r+j\\r\end{bmatrix}_qF^{(r+j)}$. These are Laurent identities, obtained by commuting $E$ past $F$ and applying Pascal before specialization. They verify all divided actions; the full toral characters verify the remaining generators.

The contragredient action $(x\varphi)(u)=\varphi(S(x)u)$ defines $
abla(a)$; its weights are the negatives of the original weights and its toral character at weight $m$ is the full character at $m$, by substituting $K^{-1}$ in the generic toral product. Double duality is identified by $K$, since $S^2=\operatorname{Ad}K$. A map $\Delta(a)	o
abla(b)$ vanishes for $a>b$ because the generating weight-$a$ vector has nowhere to go. For $a<b$, dualizing gives a map $\Delta(b)	o
abla(a)$, also zero. For $a=b$, step 1.1 maps onto the one-dimensional highest line of $
abla(a)$, and every map is determined by that line. This proves the Hom formula.

Work integrally over $A=\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$ in the quantum plane $P=A\langle x,y\rangle/(yx-vxy)$. Let $x,y$ have weights $1,-1$, $Ex=0$, $Ey=x$, $Fx=y$, $Fy=0$. The coproduct of [F1] preserves the relation: $E(yx-vxy)=vx^2-vx^2=0$ and $F(yx-vxy)=vy^2-vy^2=0$. On $P_n$, with basis $X_j=x^{n-j}y^j$, direct induction gives $E^{(r)}X_j=\begin{bmatrix}j\\r\end{bmatrix}_vX_{j-r}$ and $F^{(r)}X_j=\begin{bmatrix}n-j\\r\end{bmatrix}_vX_{j+r}$. These matrices and the full toral characters are Laurent integral. This is the dual Weyl lattice: if $w_j=(v_{n-j})^*$ in $\Delta(n)^\vee$, then $Ew_j=-v^{n-2j+2}[j]w_{j-1}$ and $Fw_j=-v^{-n+2j}[n-j]w_{j+1}$. Rescale by $c_0=1$, $c_j/c_{j-1}=-v^{-n+2j-2}$; the resulting coefficients are $[j]$ and $[n-j]$. The same calculation for divided powers proves the asserted integral identification.

For $a,b\ge1$, multiplication and insertion of the invariant tensor $x\otimes y-v^{-1}y\otimes x$ give a sequence $0\longrightarrow P_{a-1}\otimes P_{b-1}\xrightarrow{i}P_a\otimes P_b\xrightarrow{\mu}P_{a+b}\longrightarrow0,$ where $i(f\otimes g)=fx\otimes yg-v^{-1}fy\otimes xg$. Both maps are module maps by the module-algebra identities of step 3.1; invariance for higher divided powers follows from their integral matrices, or directly from their weight shifts on the two-factor tensor. Also $\mu i=0$ by $yx=vxy$. Here is exactness over $A$, before any root specialization. For $f_i=x^{a-1-i}y^i$ and $g_j=x^{b-1-j}y^j$, $i(f_i\otimes g_j)=v^{i+b-1-j}X_i\otimes Y_{j+1}-v^{-1}X_{i+1}\otimes Y_j.$ For each fixed $i+j$ these are adjacent differences along the consecutive path of target basis pairs, with unit coefficients. Successively eliminating from its first vertex proves independence and a free rank-one quotient. Multiplication sends each target vertex to a unit multiple of the same monomial, so it identifies this quotient with that monomial line. This proves exactness and freeness in every degree. It therefore remains exact at every specialization. When $a=0$ or $b=0$, $P_0=A$ is the tensor unit and the assertion is immediate. Iterating gives the dual-Weyl factors $a+b,a+b-2,\ldots,|a-b|$; dualizing reverses tensor order and gives the Weyl factors. Tensoring finite filtrations is exact over $\mathbb C$, proving tensor closure of both filtration classes and hence of tiltings.

Consider $0\to\nabla(b)\to M\to\Delta(a)\to0$. If $a\ge b$, its support is $[-a,a]$. A weight-$a$ lift of the quotient generator is highest by support; step 1.1 supplies a map $\Delta(a)\to M$ whose composite with the quotient fixes that generator and is the identity. This splits the sequence. If $a<b$, dualizing gives the already proved case with $a,b$ interchanged. This proves Ext vanishing. Induction along two finite filtrations gives the same splitting/lifting property with a Weyl-filtered first end and dual-Weyl-filtered second end: at each filtration step lift across the preceding short exact sequence, whose obstruction is an extension of the displayed type; its splitting removes that obstruction. Equivalently, applying the elementary Hom-extension exact sequence at each step gives $\operatorname{Ext}^1(D,N)=0$ for every such pair $D,N$.

Let $M$ be Weyl-filtered with maximal label $a$. Its support is $[-a,a]$. An occurrence of a quotient $\Delta(a)$ can be moved to the bottom of the filtration: lift its weight-$a$ generator across the preceding submodule and apply step 1.1, splitting that extension. Repeating for all occurrences gives the injective evaluation map $\Delta(a)\otimes_{\mathbb C}M_a\to M$, whose image is the sum of all maps from $\Delta(a)$ and whose quotient is Weyl-filtered with labels below $a$. It is injective because after these splittings it is precisely the direct sum of the top standard factors, each with a one-dimensional highest line. Any idempotent $e$ on $M$ preserves this image and acts there as $1\otimes e_a$. Its image and kernel therefore have top submodules that are sums of $\Delta(a)$'s, and their quotients are summands of the lower-label filtered quotient. Induction on the maximal label shows both are Weyl-filtered. Duality gives the corresponding assertion for dual-Weyl filtrations. Thus every summand of a tilting is tilting.

The module $V=\Delta(1)$ is its own dual Weyl, as the rescaling of step 3.1 shows at $n=1$. Its powers are tilting by step 4.1. Recursively splitting a finite-dimensional module into nontrivial direct sums terminates by dimension, giving an indecomposable decomposition. Summand closure makes these tiltings. Exactly one summand of $V^{\otimes a}$ has weight $a$, whose whole space is one-dimensional; denote it by $T(a)$. For a finite-dimensional indecomposable module, an endomorphism $h$ is either invertible or nilpotent: for large $N$, stabilized kernel and image give $M=\ker h^N\oplus\operatorname{im}h^N$. Consequently an endomorphism nonzero on a preserved one-dimensional highest line is invertible.

Let $M$ be any indecomposable finite tilting, of maximal label $a$. Step 6.1 embeds $\Delta(a)\otimes M_a$ into $M$, with lower-label Weyl-filtered quotient. Choose a vector and linear functional on $M_a$ pairing to $1$. They define maps between the standard submodules of $T(a)$ and $M$. Step 5.1 extends them to maps $f:T(a)\to M$ and $g:M\to T(a)$, because the source quotients are Weyl-filtered and the targets dual-Weyl-filtered. The composite $gf$ fixes the highest line, hence is invertible by step 7.1. Thus $T(a)$ is a nonzero summand of $M$; indecomposability forces an isomorphism. It also forces $\dim M_a=1$, proves uniqueness for each $a$, and distinguishes different $a$ by their maximal integral weights. Decomposing any finite tilting proves all the asserted classification and generation claims. The choices here concern individual finite-dimensional vector spaces and terminating finite decompositions, not a choice axiom.

citations.quote: For basis diagrams $D:m\to n$ and $E:n\to p$, stack $E$ above $D$ and identify the $n$ matching boundary points. The resulting finite graph has degree two at each identified point, where degree means the number of incident arcs. Each component is a path joining two exterior boundary points or a closed cycle. Remove every cycle and multiply the remaining exterior matching by $\delta^c$, where $c$ is the number of removed cycles. Denote this output by $E\circ D$ and extend the rule $R$-bilinearly to a map $M_R(n,p)\times M_R(m,n)\to M_R(m,p)$. A following result proves closure of these operations on the diagram modules and the category axioms.

For every commutative ring $R$, loop value $\delta\in R$, and objects $m,n,p,q\ge0$, the raw diagram data of [[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-category]] form a strict monoidal category $\mathcal{TL}_R(\delta)$ with hom-modules $M_R(m,n)$ and the stated $R$-bilinear stacking composition. Composition is associative, the identity diagrams are two-sided identities, and horizontal juxtaposition is a strict monoidal bifunctor with unit object $0$. Consequently $\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{TL}_R(\delta)}(n)=\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$ is a unital associative $R$-algebra whose underlying $R$-module is free on its noncrossing pairing diagrams.

derivations.claim: For basis diagrams $D,E:n\to n$, closing the stack $DE$ makes a finite graph whose vertices are glued endpoints and whose components are circles. Moving the cut between the $D$-layer and the $E$-layer changes the cyclic order in which the same two layers are read but neither the component partition nor the number of circles. Hence the closed graph of $DE$ and that of $ED$ have the same number of circles. Definition [F3] assigns both the same power of $\delta$, so $\operatorname{Tr}_n(DE)=\operatorname{Tr}_n(ED)$. Bilinearity extends this equality to arbitrary $x,y$.

In the closure of $D\otimes1_1$, the extra vertical strand closes to one circle disjoint from every component of the closure of $D$. Thus the closed graph has exactly $c(D)+1$ circles; its value is $\delta^{c(D)+1}=\delta\operatorname{Tr}_n(D)$, an identity valid also at $\delta=0$.

In the closure of $(D\otimes1_1)U_n$, the cap and cup of $U_n$ reconnect the added strand to the final old strand. Following the two arcs through the stack shows they form part of the same exterior-to-exterior path that was closed in $D$; they create no separate circle. Every other component is unchanged. The circle count is therefore $c(D)$, proving $\operatorname{Tr}_{n+1}((D\otimes1)U_n)=\operatorname{Tr}_n(D)$. Bilinearity gives the result for $x$.

By [F3], $\operatorname{ptr}_n(h)$ is obtained by adding the rightmost cup, stacking $h$ on the enlarged graph, and then joining the rightmost pair by the cap. Closing the remaining $n-1$ strands produces exactly the same finite graph as closing $h(x\otimes1)$ after the same $x$ has been stacked on the first $n-1$ strands. The two closures therefore have equal circle counts and equal powers of $\delta$ for each basis pair $(h,x)$. Bilinearity proves the partial-trace identity. Together with steps 1.1–1.3 this proves all claims.
