Fix an integer $\ell\ge3$ and set $q=e^{\pi i/\ell}$, so the multiplicative order of $q^2$ is $\ell$. Use the divided-power integral form of [[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]] from [[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]], specialized by $v\mapsto q$ to $\mathbb C$. In type $A_1$, write $K=K_h$ and $E,F$ for the rank-one generators. The convention is

$$KEK^{-1}=q^2E,\qquad KFK^{-1}=q^{-2}F,\qquad [E,F]=\frac{K-K^{-1}}{q-q^{-1}},$$

$$\Delta(K)=K\otimes K,\qquad \Delta(E)=E\otimes K+1\otimes E,\qquad \Delta(F)=F\otimes1+K^{-1}\otimes F.$$

This is the Sawin coproduct, rather than the inverse-$K$ coproduct in [[thm-the-drinfeld-jimbo-formulas-define-a-hopf-algebra]]. Its counit is $\varepsilon(K)=1$, $\varepsilon(E)=\varepsilon(F)=0$ and its antipode is $S(E)=-EK^{-1}$, $S(F)=-KF$, $S(K)=K^{-1}$. The exact integral transport is from the library algebra with opposite coproduct, by $E_{\rm target}=KE_{\rm lib}$, $F_{\rm target}=F_{\rm lib}K^{-1}$ and $K_{\rm target}=K_{\rm lib}$. Substituting these generators gives the displayed coproduct and unchanged mixed relation. On divided powers the formulas are $E_{\rm target}^{(r)}=v^{-r(r-1)}K^rE_{\rm lib}^{(r)}$ and $F_{\rm target}^{(r)}=v^{r(r-1)}F_{\rm lib}^{(r)}K^{-r}$; the inverse formulas also have Laurent-monomial coefficients, so the integral lattice and toral generators are preserved.

The Lusztig specialization includes all divided powers $E^{(r)},F^{(r)}$ and the toral quantum binomials; this is the divided-power form, not the small quantum group. A finite-dimensional module is **type 1** when it carries its integral-weight grading $M=\bigoplus_{m\in\mathbb Z}M_m$ with $K|_{M_m}=q^m$, the full toral character $T_{c,t}|_{M_m}=\begin{bmatrix}m+c\\t\end{bmatrix}_q I$ for every $c\in\mathbb Z$ and $t\ge0$, and $E^{(r)}M_m\subseteq M_{m+2r}$, $F^{(r)}M_m\subseteq M_{m-2r}$. The binomial is its Laurent-polynomial specialization, including negative upper indices. The grading is part of the data and is not collapsed when distinct weights have the same $K$ eigenvalue. Every module intertwiner preserves it: for $m<n$, $T_{-m,n-m}$ has eigenvalues $0$ and $1$ on weights $m$ and $n$.

For $a\ge0$, the Weyl module $\Delta(a)$ has basis $v_0,\ldots,v_a$ and actions

$$Kv_j=q^{a-2j}v_j,\qquad E^{(r)}v_j=\begin{bmatrix}a-j+r\\r\end{bmatrix}_qv_{j-r},\qquad F^{(r)}v_j=\begin{bmatrix}j+r\\r\end{bmatrix}_qv_{j+r},$$

where the Gaussian binomials are the Laurent-polynomial specializations of [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]], and $v_j=0$ outside $0\le j\le a$. Its dual is the dual Weyl module $\nabla(a)=\Delta(a)^\vee$. A **Weyl filtration** (respectively dual-Weyl filtration) is a finite submodule filtration whose successive quotients are modules $\Delta(a)$ (respectively $\nabla(a)$). A **tilting module** is a module with both filtrations.

Take $s=e^{\pi i/(2\ell)}$, so $s^2=q$. The ribbon category is the full weight-lattice extension $\mathcal U_s^\dagger(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ of this Lusztig form, not its root-lattice restriction. Its toral factor is the completed function algebra on the weight lattice $P=\mathbb Z\omega$, acting on each weight space by its weight character. Before specialization, the rank-one universal $R$-matrix is the Sawin weight-lattice expression

$R=D\sum_{r\ge0}q^{r(r+1)/2}(1-q^{-2})^r[r]_q!E^{(r)}\otimes F^{(r)},\qquad D|_{M_m\otimes N_n}=s^{mn}.$

interpreted in the completed tensor product; at the root it means the image of the integral completed form, not termwise division by a vanishing $[r]_q!$. In ordinary powers the coefficient is $q^{r(r-1)/2}(q-q^{-1})^r/[r]_q!$; changing to two divided powers multiplies that coefficient by $([r]_q!)^2$. Thus the displayed divided-power coefficient is Laurent integral and vanishes for $r\ge\ell$ after specialization. The toral factor is the weight pairing, fixed explicitly by $D$ above. The pivotal map is $j_M(x)(\varphi)=\varphi(Kx)$ and the twist is $\theta=u^{-1}j$ for the Drinfeld map $u$. The object class of this page is the full subcategory of finite-dimensional integrable type-1 tilting modules for this weight-lattice ribbon extension. No assertion about semisimplicity or the trace radical is part of this definition.

Use the full integral-weight divided-power category of [[def-temperley-lieb-rank-one-lusztig-tilting-category]], with $q=e^{\pi i/\ell}$ and every $\ell\ge3$. The displayed strings define $\Delta(a)$, and $\nabla(a)=\Delta(a)^\vee$. For all $a,b\ge0$,

$$\dim\operatorname{Hom}(\Delta(a),\nabla(b))=\delta_{ab},\qquad \operatorname{Ext}^1(\Delta(a),\nabla(b))=0.$$

Here Ext vanishing means that every short exact sequence in the finite-dimensional full-weight category with those end terms splits. The tensor product $\Delta(a)\otimes\Delta(b)$ has one Weyl factor of each label $a+b,a+b-2,\ldots,|a-b|$, and the analogous dual-Weyl assertion holds. Both filtration classes are closed under direct summands. Thus tiltings are closed under tensor products, duals and direct summands. For every $a\ge0$ there is exactly one indecomposable tilting $T(a)$ of highest weight $a$; its weight-$a$ space is one-dimensional, and it occurs as a summand of $V^{\otimes a}$, where $V=\Delta(1)$. Every finite tilting is a finite direct sum of these $T(a)$, so the additive idempotent-complete tensor category generated by $V$ is the entire tilting category.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit and $\delta\in R$. Define the quantum integers by

$$[0]_\delta=0,\qquad [1]_\delta=1,\qquad [r+1]_\delta=\delta[r]_\delta-[r-1]_\delta\quad(r\ge1).$$

The **quantum characteristic** of $(R,\delta)$ is the least positive integer $\ell$ with $[\ell]_\delta=0$, if one exists, and $\ell=\infty$ otherwise. No element of $R$ is inverted in this definition.

For $q\in\mathbb C^\times$ and $\delta=q+q^{-1}$, write $[r]_q=[r]_\delta$. If $q\ne\pm1$, this agrees with $(q^r-q^{-r})/(q-q^{-1})$; at $q=\pm1$ the recurrence gives $[r]_q=rq^{r-1}$. For complex-parameter classification, write $\kappa=\operatorname{ord}(q^2)$, with $\kappa=\infty$ when $q^2$ has infinite order. If $q\ne\pm1$, the quantum characteristic equals $\kappa$ when $\kappa<\infty$ and is $\infty$ otherwise. At $q=\pm1$, $\kappa=1$ but the complex quantum characteristic is $\infty$, because $[r]_q=rq^{r-1}\ne0$ for every positive $r$.

For a field $K$ of positive characteristic $p$, set $p(0)=1$ and, when $\ell<\infty$, set $p(i)=\ell p^{i-1}$ for $i\ge1$. In characteristic zero and finite $\ell$, the finite digit scale is $p(1)=\ell$; the separate characteristic-zero criterion below uses $a\ell-1$ for arbitrary positive integers $a$. If $\ell=\infty$, every finite index is already in the range $n<\ell$.

Fix a rigid monoidal category with chosen left duals. For a morphism
$a:X\to X^{\vee\vee}$, the **left categorical trace** of $a$ is the endomorphism
of the unit

$$\operatorname{Tr}_L(a):\mathbf 1\xrightarrow{\operatorname{coev}_X}X\otimes X^\vee\xrightarrow{a\otimes1_{X^\vee}}X^{\vee\vee}\otimes X^\vee\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_{X^\vee}}\mathbf 1.$$

For a morphism $b:X^{\vee\vee}\to X$, the **right categorical trace** of $b$ is

$$\operatorname{Tr}_R(b):\mathbf 1\xrightarrow{\operatorname{coev}_{X^\vee}}X^\vee\otimes X^{\vee\vee}\xrightarrow{1_{X^\vee}\otimes b}X^\vee\otimes X\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_X}\mathbf 1.$$

So a bare endomorphism $X\to X$ is not yet an input to categorical trace; one
first needs a comparison between $X$ and a double dual.

Let $(-)^{\vee\vee}$ be the monoidal endofunctor of
[[thm-the-double-dual-is-a-monoidal-functor]].

A **pivotal structure** on a rigid monoidal category is an isomorphism of
monoidal functors

$$a:\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal C}\xrightarrow{\sim}(-)^{\vee\vee}.$$

Equivalently, it is a natural family of isomorphisms
$a_X:X\xrightarrow{\sim}X^{\vee\vee}$ such that

$$a_{X\otimes Y}=a_X\otimes a_Y,\qquad a_{\mathbf 1}=1_{\mathbf 1}$$

after transporting along the monoidal structure of the double-dual functor.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a rigid monoidal category, let $a:X\to X^{\vee\vee}$ and $b:Y\to Y^{\vee\vee}$, and suppress the monoidal and chosen-dual comparison maps. For $s\in\operatorname{End}(\mathbf1)$ write $\ell_Z(s)$ and $r_Z(s)$ for its left and right actions on $Z$, transported from $s\otimes1_Z$ and $1_Z\otimes s$ by the unit constraints.

1. $\operatorname{Tr}_L(a)=\operatorname{Tr}_R(a^\vee)$.
2. If the category is additive, then
   $\operatorname{Tr}_L(a\oplus b)=\operatorname{Tr}_L(a)+\operatorname{Tr}_L(b)$.
3. The general tensor formula is
   $\operatorname{Tr}_L(a\otimes b)=\operatorname{Tr}_L(r_{X^{\vee\vee}}(\operatorname{Tr}_L(b))a)$.
   If $r_{X^{\vee\vee}}(\operatorname{Tr}_L(b))=\ell_{X^{\vee\vee}}(\operatorname{Tr}_L(b))$, this becomes
   $\operatorname{Tr}_L(a\otimes b)=\operatorname{Tr}_L(a)\operatorname{Tr}_L(b)$.
   In particular multiplicativity holds when every unit scalar has equal left and right actions on every object. This condition holds in a braided category, and also in a $k$-linear monoidal category with $k$-bilinear tensor product and $\operatorname{End}(\mathbf1)=k$.
4. For every endomorphism $c:X\to X$,
   $\operatorname{Tr}_L(ac)=\operatorname{Tr}_L(c^{\vee\vee}a)$.

The corresponding right-trace duality, additivity and cyclicity statements hold. For right-trace inputs $p:X^{\vee\vee}\to X$ and $q:Y^{\vee\vee}\to Y$, the general tensor formula is

$$\operatorname{Tr}_R(p\otimes q)=\operatorname{Tr}_R(q\ell_{Y^{\vee\vee}}(\operatorname{Tr}_R(p))).$$

It reduces to multiplicativity under the analogous equality of scalar actions, in particular under either sufficient condition above.

derivations.claim: We first prove the needed zero/nonzero Gaussian rule. Put $z=v^2$; then $\begin{bmatrix}N\\J\end{bmatrix}_v=v^{-J(N-J)}{N\brack J}_z$. The generating identity $\prod_{r=0}^{N-1}(1+z^rt)=\sum_Jz^{J(J-1)/2}{N\brack J}_zt^J$ follows by multiplying one factor and applying Pascal. At primitive $\ell$th $z$, a full block has product $1-(-t)^\ell$. For $N=A\ell+B$ and $J=C\ell+D$, $0\le B,D<\ell$, the product is $(1-(-t)^\ell)^A\prod_{r=0}^{B-1}(1+z^rt)$. Its degree-$J$ coefficient is zero when $D>B$, and otherwise is a nonzero root-of-unity factor times $\binom AC{B\brack D}_z$, provided $0\le C\le A$. The residual Gaussian is nonzero because its numerator and denominator involve only nonzero factors of indices below $\ell$. Thus $\begin{bmatrix}N\\J\end{bmatrix}_q$ has exactly that zero/nonzero rule; no phase convention is needed below.

The Weyl module $\Delta(n)$ is simple for $0\le n<\ell$ and for $n=a\ell-1$, $a\ge1$. Every nonzero submodule contains a nonzero weight vector because full toral characters separate weights. Its weight spaces are one-dimensional, so it contains some $v_j$. The coefficient in $E^{(j)}v_j=\begin{bmatrix}n\\j\end{bmatrix}_qv_0$ is nonzero: for $n<\ell$ use the product formula, and for $n=a\ell-1$ use step 1.1 with residual digit $\ell-1$. Thus it contains $v_0$ and every $F^{(k)}v_0=v_k$. The dual is simple with the same highest weight; the bounded-highest-vector map in [F2] is a nonzero isomorphism $\Delta(n)\to\nabla(n)$. These modules are therefore tilting and equal to $T(n)$ by [F2].

Fix $a\ge1$, $0\le b\le\ell-2$, and put $m=a\ell+b$, $m'=a\ell-b-2$. The module $X=\Delta(a\ell-1)\otimes\Delta(b+1)$ is tilting by step 2.1 and [F2]. Its Weyl labels are $n_j=m-2j$, $0\le j\le b+1$, each once. Use the central quantum Casimir $C=(q-q^{-1})^2FE+qK+q^{-1}K^{-1}$. Its commutator with $E$ vanishes by substituting $[F,E]=-(K-K^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})$ and $KE=q^2EK$. The involution $E\leftrightarrow F$, $K\leftrightarrow K^{-1}$ fixes $C$ (use the mixed relation), so its commutator with $F$ vanishes too. It commutes with every divided power and toral binomial: the generic commutators vanish in the integral subalgebra before specialization. Its scalar on $\Delta(n)$ is $c_n=q^{n+1}+q^{-n-1}$, evaluated on the generating highest vector. Now $c_{n_j}=(-1)^a(z_j+z_j^{-1})$ with $z_j=q^{b+1-2j}$. Since $0<b+1<\ell$ and $-(b+1)\le b+1-2j\le b+1$, equality with $c_m$ occurs exactly at $j=0,b+1$: equality of $z+z^{-1}$ means $z=q^{b+1}$ or $q^{-b-1}$. The generalized $c_m$-eigenspace $Y$ is a module summand. Primary-decomposition polynomial projectors preserve submodules and quotients, so applying this projector to a Weyl filtration retains precisely $\Delta(m)$ and $\Delta(m')$. Thus $Y$ is tilting with character $\chi(m)+\chi(m')$.

To prove $Y$ indecomposable, first show $\Delta(m)
ot\cong
abla(m)$. The vector $v_{b+1}$ is highest of weight $m'$: for $1\le r\le b+1$, its $E^{(r)}$ coefficient is $ egin{bmatrix}a\ell-1+r\r\end{bmatrix}_q=0$, because its numerator contains $[a\ell]$ and its denominator indices are below $\ell$; larger $r$ give zero by the string convention. Its generated submodule is spanned by $F^{(j)}v_{b+1}$. Terms with $j>m'$ vanish. Indeed a possibly nonzero basis term requires $j\le a\ell-1$; in the remaining interval write $j=(a-1)\ell+d$ with $\ell-b-1\le d<\ell$. The upper residual digit of $b+1+j$ is $b+1+d-\ell<d$, so step 1.1 gives $ egin{bmatrix}b+1+j\j\end{bmatrix}_q=0$. The generated submodule is therefore supported on $[-m',m']$. The highest-vector property [F2] gives a nonzero map $\Delta(m')	o\Delta(m)$. Hom orthogonality in [F2] forbids this if $\Delta(m)\cong
abla(m)$, since $m'<m$.

Decompose $Y$ into indecomposable tiltings using [F2]. Its unique highest-weight-$m$ summand is $T(m)$. Its only two Weyl factors are those found in step 3.1, each once. If $Y$ were decomposable, the top summand would have the sole Weyl factor $\Delta(m)$ and its complement the sole factor $\Delta(m')$. Then $T(m)=\Delta(m)$ would be tilting. Weyl characters are triangular and linearly independent, so a dual-Weyl filtration of character $\chi(m)$ has the sole factor $\nabla(m)$, contradicting step 4.1. Hence $Y=T(m)$, proving the two-factor character formula. Step 2.1 gives the Steinberg formula.

Expanding coevaluation in a weight basis, [F4] gives $\dim_q\Delta(n)=\sum_{j=0}^nq^{n-2j}=[n+1]_q$. The two characters in step 5.1 have dimensions $[a\ell+b+1]_q=(-1)^a[b+1]_q$ and $[a\ell-b-1]_q=(-1)^{a+1}[b+1]_q$, which cancel. The Steinberg dimension is $[a\ell]_q=0$. For retained labels [F3] gives $[m+1]_q>0$.

Let $f$ be an endomorphism of an indecomposable $T(m)$. Over $\mathbb C$ it has an eigenvalue $\lambda$. Then $f-\lambda I$ is not invertible and is nilpotent by the Fitting argument of [F2]. It preserves each integral weight space; on that space it has ordinary trace zero, so also weighted trace zero after multiplication by $q^{\text{weight}}$. Therefore $\operatorname{tr}(Kf)=\lambda\dim_qT(m)$. By step 6.1 this vanishes for every $m\ge\ell-1$ and every $f$. In particular all test composites have zero trace, so the identity is negligible. Finite sums remain negligible because trace is the sum of diagonal-block traces. For the retained labels simplicity follows from step 2.1 and nonzero dimension from step 6.1. This proves all claims, without a linkage theorem or an oddness hypothesis.

Then $p_2^2=p_2$ follows from $U_1^2=\delta U_1$, $U_1p_2=p_2U_1=0$, and its identity coefficient is $1$; it is nonzero because the identity and cup-cap diagrams are distinct basis vectors. The recursion gives $P_r=Q-\mu QaQ$. The supports of $Q$ and $b$ are disjoint, so they commute; using $b^2=\delta b$ and $bab=b$ from [F2] gives $bP_rb=\delta Qb-\mu QbabQ=(\delta-\mu)Qb=([r+1]/[r])Qb$, where [F3] proves the last equality. Since $QP_r=P_r$ and $Qb=bQ$, this is the absorption identity needed below.

Set $X=P_rbP_r$ and $c=[r]/[r+1]$. Step 1.1 gives $X^2=P_r(bP_rb)P_r=([r+1]/[r])X$, hence $p_{r+1}^2=(P_r-cX)^2=P_r-2cX+c^2X^2=P_r-cX=p_{r+1}$. If $D$ is any nonidentity basis diagram, [F4] writes it as a nonempty word in the generators. Expanding any $x\in\mathrm{TL}_n$ in the diagram basis gives $p_nxp_n=\lambda_xp_n$ for a scalar $\lambda_x\in R$, hence $p_n\mathrm{TL}_np_n=Rp_n$. If $p_n'$ is another idempotent with identity coefficient $1$ and the same annihilation, write $p_n=1+m$, $p_n'=1+m'$ with $m,m'$ linear combinations of nonidentity diagrams. The equalities $p_n'p_n=p_n$ and $p_n'p_n=p_n'$ follow respectively from $m'p_n=0$ and $p_n'm=0$; therefore $p_n=p_n'$.

For $n\ge2$, write $p_n=P-([n-1]/[n])P U_{n-1}P$ with $P=p_{n-1}\otimes1$. Closing the last identity strand gives $\operatorname{ptr}_n(P)=\delta p_{n-1}$ by [F6]. Fix an integer $\ell\ge3$ and set $q=e^{\pi i/\ell}$, so the multiplicative order of $q^2$ is $\ell$. Use the divided-power integral form of [[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]] from [[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]], specialized by $v\mapsto q$ to $\mathbb C$. In type $A_1$, write $K=K_h$ and $E,F$ for the rank-one generators. The convention is

$$KEK^{-1}=q^2E,\qquad KFK^{-1}=q^{-2}F,\qquad [E,F]=\frac{K-K^{-1}}{q-q^{-1}},$$

$$\Delta(K)=K\otimes K,\qquad \Delta(E)=E\otimes K+1\otimes E,\qquad \Delta(F)=F\otimes1+K^{-1}\otimes F.$$

This is the Sawin coproduct, rather than the inverse-$K$ coproduct in [[thm-the-drinfeld-jimbo-formulas-define-a-hopf-algebra]]. Its counit is $\varepsilon(K)=1$, $\varepsilon(E)=\varepsilon(F)=0$ and its antipode is $S(E)=-EK^{-1}$, $S(F)=-KF$, $S(K)=K^{-1}$. The exact integral transport is from the library algebra with opposite coproduct, by $E_{\rm target}=KE_{\rm lib}$, $F_{\rm target}=F_{\rm lib}K^{-1}$ and $K_{\rm target}=K_{\rm lib}$. Substituting these generators gives the displayed coproduct and unchanged mixed relation. On divided powers the formulas are $E_{\rm target}^{(r)}=v^{-r(r-1)}K^rE_{\rm lib}^{(r)}$ and $F_{\rm target}^{(r)}=v^{r(r-1)}F_{\rm lib}^{(r)}K^{-r}$; the inverse formulas also have Laurent-monomial coefficients, so the integral lattice and toral generators are preserved.

The Lusztig specialization includes all divided powers $E^{(r)},F^{(r)}$ and the toral quantum binomials; this is the divided-power form, not the small quantum group. A finite-dimensional module is **type 1** when it carries its integral-weight grading $M=\bigoplus_{m\in\mathbb Z}M_m$ with $K|_{M_m}=q^m$, the full toral character $T_{c,t}|_{M_m}=\begin{bmatrix}m+c\\t\end{bmatrix}_q I$ for every $c\in\mathbb Z$ and $t\ge0$, and $E^{(r)}M_m\subseteq M_{m+2r}$, $F^{(r)}M_m\subseteq M_{m-2r}$. The binomial is its Laurent-polynomial specialization, including negative upper indices. The grading is part of the data and is not collapsed when distinct weights have the same $K$ eigenvalue. Every module intertwiner preserves it: for $m<n$, $T_{-m,n-m}$ has eigenvalues $0$ and $1$ on weights $m$ and $n$.

For $a\ge0$, the Weyl module $\Delta(a)$ has basis $v_0,\ldots,v_a$ and actions

$$Kv_j=q^{a-2j}v_j,\qquad E^{(r)}v_j=\begin{bmatrix}a-j+r\\r\end{bmatrix}_qv_{j-r},\qquad F^{(r)}v_j=\begin{bmatrix}j+r\\r\end{bmatrix}_qv_{j+r},$$

where the Gaussian binomials are the Laurent-polynomial specializations of [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]], and $v_j=0$ outside $0\le j\le a$. Its dual is the dual Weyl module $\nabla(a)=\Delta(a)^\vee$. A **Weyl filtration** (respectively dual-Weyl filtration) is a finite submodule filtration whose successive quotients are modules $\Delta(a)$ (respectively $\nabla(a)$). A **tilting module** is a module with both filtrations.

Take $s=e^{\pi i/(2\ell)}$, so $s^2=q$. The ribbon category is the full weight-lattice extension $\mathcal U_s^\dagger(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ of this Lusztig form, not its root-lattice restriction. Its toral factor is the completed function algebra on the weight lattice $P=\mathbb Z\omega$, acting on each weight space by its weight character. Before specialization, the rank-one universal $R$-matrix is the Sawin weight-lattice expression

$R=D\sum_{r\ge0}q^{r(r+1)/2}(1-q^{-2})^r[r]_q!E^{(r)}\otimes F^{(r)},\qquad D|_{M_m\otimes N_n}=s^{mn}.$

interpreted in the completed tensor product; at the root it means the image of the integral completed form, not termwise division by a vanishing $[r]_q!$. In ordinary powers the coefficient is $q^{r(r-1)/2}(q-q^{-1})^r/[r]_q!$; changing to two divided powers multiplies that coefficient by $([r]_q!)^2$. Thus the displayed divided-power coefficient is Laurent integral and vanishes for $r\ge\ell$ after specialization. The toral factor is the weight pairing, fixed explicitly by $D$ above. The pivotal map is $j_M(x)(\varphi)=\varphi(Kx)$ and the twist is $\theta=u^{-1}j$ for the Drinfeld map $u$. The object class of this page is the full subcategory of finite-dimensional integrable type-1 tilting modules for this weight-lattice ribbon extension. No assertion about semisimplicity or the trace radical is part of this definition.

Use the full integral-weight divided-power category of [[def-temperley-lieb-rank-one-lusztig-tilting-category]], with $q=e^{\pi i/\ell}$ and every $\ell\ge3$. The displayed strings define $\Delta(a)$, and $\nabla(a)=\Delta(a)^\vee$. For all $a,b\ge0$,

$$\dim\operatorname{Hom}(\Delta(a),\nabla(b))=\delta_{ab},\qquad \operatorname{Ext}^1(\Delta(a),\nabla(b))=0.$$

Here Ext vanishing means that every short exact sequence in the finite-dimensional full-weight category with those end terms splits. The tensor product $\Delta(a)\otimes\Delta(b)$ has one Weyl factor of each label $a+b,a+b-2,\ldots,|a-b|$, and the analogous dual-Weyl assertion holds. Both filtration classes are closed under direct summands. Thus tiltings are closed under tensor products, duals and direct summands. For every $a\ge0$ there is exactly one indecomposable tilting $T(a)$ of highest weight $a$; its weight-$a$ space is one-dimensional, and it occurs as a summand of $V^{\otimes a}$, where $V=\Delta(1)$. Every finite tilting is a finite direct sum of these $T(a)$, so the additive idempotent-complete tensor category generated by $V$ is the entire tilting category.

Let $q=e^{\pi i/\ell}$, $\ell\ge3$, and use the full-weight category of [[def-temperley-lieb-rank-one-lusztig-tilting-category]]. Write $T(m)$ for the indecomposable tilting of highest weight $m$ and $\chi(m)=\sum_{j=0}^m e^{m-2j}$. For $a\ge1$ and $0\le b\le\ell-2$,

$$\operatorname{ch}T(a\ell+b)=\chi(a\ell+b)+\chi(a\ell-b-2),\qquad \operatorname{ch}T(a\ell-1)=\chi(a\ell-1).$$

Also $T(m)=\Delta(m)=\nabla(m)$ for $0\le m<\ell$. With the positive $K$ pivotal map, the dimension on a Weyl character is $[m+1]_q$. Consequently every $T(m)$ with $m\ge\ell-1$ has zero pivotal trace on **every** endomorphism, so its identity is negligible. In the retained range $0\le m\le\ell-2$, $T(m)$ is simple of nonzero pivotal dimension $[m+1]_q$.

Let $T$ and $I_{\mathrm{DJ}}$ be the free $\mathbb Q(q)$-algebra and defining ideal of [[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]], and write $K_i=K_{d_i h_i}$. Let $\Delta:T\to T\otimes_{\mathbb Q(q)}T$ and $\varepsilon:T\to\mathbb Q(q)$ be the algebra homomorphisms determined by

$$\Delta(K_h)=K_h\otimes K_h,\quad \Delta(E_i)=E_i\otimes K_i^{-1}+1\otimes E_i,\quad \Delta(F_i)=F_i\otimes1+K_i\otimes F_i,\quad \varepsilon(K_h)=1,\quad\varepsilon(E_i)=\varepsilon(F_i)=0.$$

Let $S:T\to T$ be the $\mathbb Q(q)$-linear algebra anti-homomorphism determined by

$$S(K_h)=K_{-h},\qquad S(E_i)=-E_iK_i,\qquad S(F_i)=-K_i^{-1}F_i.$$

Then

$$\Delta(I_{\mathrm{DJ}})\subseteq I_{\mathrm{DJ}}\otimes T+T\otimes I_{\mathrm{DJ}},\qquad \varepsilon(I_{\mathrm{DJ}})=0,\qquad S(I_{\mathrm{DJ}})\subseteq I_{\mathrm{DJ}}.$$

Hence these maps descend to $U_q(\mathfrak g)=T/I_{\mathrm{DJ}}$ and make it a Hopf algebra over $\mathbb Q(q)$ ([[def-bialgebra-counit-and-antipode]]): $\Delta$ is coassociative, $\varepsilon$ is a counit, and

$$m(S\otimes\operatorname{id})\Delta=\eta\circ\varepsilon=m(\operatorname{id}\otimes S)\Delta.$$

The antipode $S$ is unique for this multiplication, unit, coproduct and counit ([[lem-an-antipode-is-unique]]), and its square satisfies

$$S^2(E_i)=q_i^{-2}E_i,\qquad S^2(F_i)=q_i^{2}F_i,\qquad S^2(K_h)=K_h.$$

Fix a symmetrizable Cartan datum and $i\in I$, and use the conventions of [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]. Write $C_{m,r}:=\binom{m}{r}_i$, with $C_{m,r}=0$ when $r<0$ or $r>m$.

(i) **Pascal recurrences.** For $m\ge1$ and every integer $r$,

$$C_{m,r}=q_i^{-r}C_{m-1,r}+q_i^{m-r}C_{m-1,r-1}=q_i^rC_{m-1,r}+q_i^{r-m}C_{m-1,r-1}.$$

(ii) **Symmetry.** For $0\le r\le m$, $C_{m,r}=C_{m,m-r}$.

(iii) **Gauss product formula.** For every $N\ge0$, in the polynomial ring $\mathbb Q(q)[z]$,

$$\prod_{j=0}^{N-1}(1+q_i^{2j}z)=\sum_{r=0}^{N}q_i^{r(N-1)}C_{N,r}z^r.$$

Consequently, for $N\ge1$,

$$\sum_{r=0}^{N}(-1)^rq_i^{r(N-1)}C_{N,r}=0.$$

(iv) **Integrality.** For $0\le r\le m$,

$$C_{m,r}\in q_i^{-r(m-r)}\mathbb Z[q_i^2]\subseteq\mathbb Z[q_i^{\pm1}].$$

Thus every Gaussian quotient is a Laurent polynomial in $q_i$ with integer coefficients, and the Pascal recurrences hold in that Laurent polynomial ring.

An object of a monoidal category is **rigid** if it has both a left dual and a
right dual in the sense of [[def-left-dual-and-right-dual-object]].

A monoidal category is **rigid** if every object in it is rigid.

Muger's notes also use the word **autonomous** for the same condition, and
Joyal-Street use **compact** in the non-symmetric setting.

Let $(\mathcal C,\otimes,\mathbf 1,\alpha,\lambda,\rho)$ be a monoidal
category ([[def-monoidal-category]]).

A **braiding** on $\mathcal C$ is a natural isomorphism

$$c_{X,Y}:X\otimes Y\longrightarrow Y\otimes X$$

natural in both variables ([[def-natural-isomorphism]]) such that, for all
objects $X,Y,Z$,

$$\alpha_{Y,Z,X}\circ c_{X,Y\otimes Z}\circ\alpha_{X,Y,Z}=(1_Y\otimes c_{X,Z})\circ\alpha_{Y,X,Z}\circ(c_{X,Y}\otimes1_Z),$$

and

$$\alpha_{Z,X,Y}^{-1}\circ c_{X\otimes Y,Z}\circ\alpha_{X,Y,Z}^{-1}=(c_{X,Z}\otimes1_Y)\circ\alpha_{X,Z,Y}^{-1}\circ(1_X\otimes c_{Y,Z}).$$

These are the two **hexagon identities**. The invertibility of each
$c_{X,Y}$ is part of the data, not a consequence of the hexagons.

Let $(-)^{\vee\vee}$ be the monoidal endofunctor of
[[thm-the-double-dual-is-a-monoidal-functor]].

A **pivotal structure** on a rigid monoidal category is an isomorphism of
monoidal functors

$$a:\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal C}\xrightarrow{\sim}(-)^{\vee\vee}.$$

Equivalently, it is a natural family of isomorphisms
$a_X:X\xrightarrow{\sim}X^{\vee\vee}$ such that

$$a_{X\otimes Y}=a_X\otimes a_Y,\qquad a_{\mathbf 1}=1_{\mathbf 1}$$

after transporting along the monoidal structure of the double-dual functor.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a braided rigid monoidal category with braiding $c$, and
fix left duals $X^\vee$ for all objects together with the dual-morphism
operation of [[def-the-dual-of-a-morphism]].

A **twist** on $\mathcal C$ is a natural automorphism
$\theta\in\operatorname{Aut}(\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal C})$ such that

$$\theta_{X\otimes Y}=(\theta_X\otimes\theta_Y)\circ c_{Y,X}\circ c_{X,Y}$$

for all objects $X,Y$ and $\theta_{\mathbf 1}=1_{\mathbf 1}$.

A **ribbon structure** is a twist satisfying the dual-compatibility condition

$$(\theta_X)^\vee=\theta_{X^\vee}.$$

In a braided rigid monoidal category there is a natural isomorphism

$$u_X:X\to X^{\vee\vee},$$

called the **Drinfeld morphism** (or **Drinfeld isomorphism**), defined by

$$X\xrightarrow{1_X\otimes\operatorname{coev}_{X^\vee}}X\otimes X^\vee\otimes X^{\vee\vee}\xrightarrow{c_{X,X^\vee}\otimes1_{X^{\vee\vee}}}X^\vee\otimes X\otimes X^{\vee\vee}\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_X\otimes1_{X^{\vee\vee}}}X^{\vee\vee}.$$

Write

$$d_{X,Y}:X^{\vee\vee}\otimes Y^{\vee\vee}\xrightarrow{\sim}(X\otimes Y)^{\vee\vee}$$

for the monoidal comparison of the double-dual functor. Then

$$d_{X,Y}\circ(u_X\otimes u_Y)=u_{X\otimes Y}\circ c_{Y,X}\circ c_{X,Y}.$$

Thus $u$ need not be monoidal: the double braiding is precisely its
monoidality obstruction.

derivations.claim: In the basis $(v_+,v_-)$, $K=\operatorname{diag}(q,q^{-1})$, $E_{12}=1$ and $F_{21}=1$. Substitution in the coproduct shows that $w$ and $b$ are invariant for $E,F,K$. They preserve total integral weight, hence all toral binomials. Divided powers of index $r\ge3$ vanish on $V^{\otimes2}$ by weight range, and the index-$2$ actions are ordinary squares divided by nonzero $[2]$; invariance therefore holds for the full divided-power algebra. The two direct contractions $(1\otimes b)(w\otimes1)$ and $(b\otimes1)(1\otimes w)$ each send $v_\pm$ to itself. Their closed composite is $-q-q^{-1}=-\delta$. Every invariant cup and cap is a scalar multiple of these, by solving the weight-zero $E$ equation, and the snakes force the two scalars' product to be $1$; that loop cannot become $+\delta$ by rescaling. With $B=\begin{pmatrix}0&-q\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ one has $KB^t=-B$, or $b(y,Kx)=-b(x,y)$. This is the exact negative pivotal symmetry sign.

Work generically over $\mathbb Q(s)$ and put $t=q^{-2}$. In ordinary powers the nilpotent series is $f(Z)=\sum_{r\ge0}a_rZ^r$, where $a_r=q^{r(r-1)/2}(q-q^{-1})^r/[r]_q!=(q-q^{-1})^r/(r)!_t$ and $(r)!_t=\prod_{j=1}^r(1+t+\cdots+t^{j-1})$. If $AB=q^2BA$, Pascal induction gives $(A+B)^r=\sum_{i+j=r}{r\brack i}_t A^iB^j$; dividing by $(r)!_t$ proves $f(A+B)=f(A)f(B)$. On weight spaces $D_{ij}E_iD_{ij}^{-1}=E_iK_j$ and $D_{ij}F_jD_{ij}^{-1}=K_i^{-1}F_j$. Hence $(\Delta\otimes1)R=D_{13}D_{23}f(E_1K_2F_3)f(E_2F_3)=R_{13}R_{23},$ because $E_1K_2F_3$ and $E_2F_3$ $q^2$-commute and $D_{23}^{-1}F_3D_{23}=K_2F_3$. Likewise $(1\otimes\Delta)R=D_{12}D_{13}f(E_1K_2^{-1}F_3)f(E_1F_2)=R_{13}R_{12},$ using $K_2^{-1}F_2=q^2F_2K_2^{-1}$ and $D_{12}^{-1}E_1D_{12}=E_1K_2^{-1}$. These are coefficientwise identities of finite series on any fixed tensor powers.

In the ordered tensor basis $(++,+-,-+,--)$, $U=-wb$ has its nonzero middle block $\begin{pmatrix}q&-1\\-1&q^{-1}\end{pmatrix}$. Thus $U^2=\delta U$. The snakes give $(wb)_1(wb)_2(wb)_1=(wb)_1$, so also $U_1U_2U_1=U_1$; disjoint operators commute. The finite series on $V^{\otimes2}$ is $R=D(1+(q-q^{-1})E\otimes F)$, giving $c=sI-s^{-1}U$ and inverse $s^{-1}I-sU$. It is a full-algebra intertwiner by direct $E,F,K$ substitution and the divided-power/toral check of step 1.1. Its eigenvalues on $\ker U$ and $\operatorname{im}U$ are $s$ and $-s^{-3}$, respectively; $\operatorname{im}U=\mathbb Cw$ is the trivial channel. The complementary three-dimensional highest-weight string is $\Delta(2)$ by [F2]. Substitution gives $qU-I=-s c^{-1}$ and the stated Hecke eigenvalues. The adjacent TL relations give Yang–Baxter: after expanding both triple products, the remaining coefficient is $s-s^{-1}\delta+s^{-3}=0$.

These tensor powers have explicit free integral tensor lattices. Their divided-power matrices are Laurent integral by the coproduct Gaussian expansion, and a toral binomial acts by the integral Gaussian at the total weight. All generic defining relations and associativity identities are therefore matrix identities over that lattice and remain true after specialization; this argument concerns finite matrices and needs no basis selection for an arbitrary completed algebra. Rewriting each series term as $q^{r(r+1)/2}(1-q^{-2})^r[r]_q!E^{(r)}\otimes F^{(r)}$ makes its coefficient Laurent integral. Only finitely many $r$ act by weight range, $D$ has powers $s^{mn}$, and $[r]!$ multiplies the term. Thus step 1.2 specializes at every $\ell\ge3$, including $r\ge\ell$, where the coefficient is zero. Inducting on tensor lengths identifies this finite series on $V^{\otimes m}\otimes V^{\otimes n}$ with the ordered block product of the elementary crossings of step 2.1. It is invertible and intertwines the entire specialized algebra. The block products satisfy both hexagons by partitioning their strands.

If $g:M\to M'$ and $h:N\to N'$ are module maps, they preserve integral weights and commute with every divided power. Consequently $g\otimes h$ commutes, in the typed sense, with each series term and $D$. This proves naturality with every full-algebra intertwiner directly. In particular the series and its inverse restrict to summands of tensor powers. By [F2], direct sums and such restrictions exhaust all tiltings, so invertibility, naturality and both hexagons hold throughout that category, not merely on tensor powers or on a small-quantum-group subcategory. Duals of tiltings are tilting by their two filtrations; evaluation and coevaluation for the antipode satisfy the vector-space snakes and are module maps. This proves rigidity and braiding.

Since $S^2=\operatorname{Ad}K$, $j_M(x)(\varphi)=\varphi(Kx)$ is a module map to the double dual. It is natural, invertible and monoidal because $K$ is group-like. Form $\theta=u^{-1}j$ using [F4]. On $V^*$ the matrices are $E^*=-(EK^{-1})^t$, $F^*=-(KF)^t$, with weights $-1,1$. Inserting them into the finite $R$ and the evaluation formula for $u$ gives $u_V=\operatorname{diag}(s^{-1},s^{-5})$: its second entry is $s^{-1}(1-(q-q^{-1})q^{-1})=s^{-5}$. Thus $\theta_V=s^3I$. The tensor defect in [F4] gives the balancing identity for $\theta$. Dual compatibility holds on $V$, since it is self-dual and this twist is scalar. It then holds on every tensor power: duality reverses tensor order, the two dual crossings are the reversed crossings given by the evaluation snakes, and balancing on the two factors gives the same composite on either side. Naturality extends this equality to direct sums and summands. By [F2] these are all tiltings, proving the ribbon condition.

The simple $\Delta(a)$ for $a\le\ell-1$ occurs as a highest-weight summand in $V^{\otimes a}$ by [F2]. Its highest vector is $v_+^{\otimes a}$. Every elementary crossing there acts by $s$; balancing therefore gives twist $(s^3)^a s^{a(a-1)}=s^{a(a+2)}$. Naturality and the scalar endomorphism property make this its twist on the whole simple. The values at $a=0,1,2$ give $1,s^3,s^8$. At $\ell=3$, [F2] says $\Delta(2)$ has zero endomorphism trace and is removed in the negligible quotient; it is a genuine prequotient channel, not a retained one. Finally $\operatorname{tr}(K|_V)=q+q^{-1}=\delta$, despite the self-dual loop in step 1.1 being $-\delta$. These prove all stated convention and boundary assertions.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and let $\delta\in R$. The object labels are the nonnegative integers $n=0,1,2,\ldots$. For labels $m,n$, place bottom points $b_1,\ldots,b_m$ and top points $t_1,\ldots,t_n$ along the rectangle from left to right on their respective edges. Their cyclic order is $t_1,\ldots,t_n,b_m,\ldots,b_1$. When $m=n=0$, the empty matching is included.

An $(m,n)$ **diagram** is a perfect matching of these $m+n$ boundary labels which is noncrossing: there are no four labels $a,b,c,d$ in cyclic order whose matched pairs are $\{a,c\}$ and $\{b,d\}$. A picture consists of disjoint arcs realizing the matching; equality is equality of the matching, so planar deformation that fixes the boundary does not change a diagram. For basis diagrams $D:m\to n$ and $E:n\to p$, stack $E$ above $D$ and identify the $n$ matching boundary points. The resulting finite graph has degree two at each identified point, where degree means the number of incident arcs. Each component is a path joining two exterior boundary points or a closed cycle. Remove every cycle and multiply the remaining exterior matching by $\delta^c$, where $c$ is the number of removed cycles. A following result proves closure of these operations on the diagram modules and the category axioms.

The matching $1_n:n\to n$ pairs each bottom point to the top point directly above it. Horizontal juxtaposition, with the left diagram placed first, defines $m\otimes m'=m+m'$ on object labels and $D\otimes D'$ on basis diagrams; extend it $R$-bilinearly to the modules. For $1\le i<n$, let $d_i\in M_R(n,n)$ be the diagram with a cap joining top points $i,i+1$, a cup joining bottom points $i,i+1$, and vertical through strands at every other position. $$\operatorname{Tr}_n(D)=\delta^{c(D)}$$

$$\operatorname{ptr}_n(x)=(1_{n-1}\otimes\cap)\circ(x\otimes1_1)\circ(1_{n-1}\otimes\cup),\qquad x\in\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta).$$

for $x,y\in\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$, where $U_n$ is the cup-cap generator on the last two strands of $\mathrm{TL}_{n+1}$. For $x\in\mathrm{TL}_{n-1}$ and $h\in\mathrm{TL}_n$,

In characteristic zero and finite $\ell$, the finite digit scale is $p(1)=\ell$; the separate characteristic-zero criterion below uses $a\ell-1$ for arbitrary positive integers $a$. derivations.claim: Write $E_n=\operatorname{ptr}_n$. Closing matching graphs gives three exact identities: $E_n$ is $B_{n-1}$-bilinear, $E_n(x\otimes1)=\delta x$, and $E_n(U_{n-1})=1$. Also, for $x\in B_{n-1}$, $U_{n-1}(x\otimes1)U_{n-1}=(E_{n-1}(x)\otimes1\otimes1)U_{n-1}.$ Indeed the two neighboring cups/caps close precisely the last input/output strand of $x$, leaving its other strands and the final cup/cap unchanged; every closed component contributes the same factor on both sides. For $x=1$ this gives $U_{n-1}^2=\delta U_{n-1}$, fixing the unnormalized factor. Since $B_n$ is generated by $B_{n-1}$ and $U_{n-1}$, this identity reduces every alternating word with two final generators to one with fewer such occurrences. Hence $B_n$ is spanned by $B_{n-1}+B_{n-1}U_{n-1}B_{n-1}$.

To handle arbitrary-size morphisms we give an auxiliary diagram factorization. It does not identify a positive-loop pivotal category with the quantum ribbon category. Choose $A=i e^{\pi i/(2\ell)}$, so $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$, and put $C=A\,1+A^{-1}U$. Its inverse is $A^{-1}1+AU$ because $A^2+A^{-2}+\delta=0$. The adjacent triple expansion gives Yang–Baxter, with remaining coefficient $A+A^{-1}\delta+A^{-3}=0$. Let $W_1=\cup\otimes1$ and $W_2=1\otimes\cup$. The snakes give $U_1W_1=\delta W_1$, $U_2W_1=W_2$ and $U_1W_2=W_1$, whence $C_1C_2W_1=(A^2+\delta+A^{-2})W_1+W_2=W_2,\qquad C_2C_1W_2=W_1.$ Reflection gives the two corresponding cap slides. Thus ordered block crossings $C_{r,t}:r+t\to t+r$ are natural with every matching, since cups, caps and identities generate those morphisms; linearity gives naturality with arbitrary diagram elements. Partitioning a block proves both block-crossing identities, and the triple relation identifies the ordered crossing words. All crossings used here are finite linear combinations of ordinary diagrams.

Every nonempty generator word kills $f$ on its appropriate side, so $J_m=\mathbb Cf$. The boundary partial trace is $E_m(f)=\frac{[\ell]}{[\ell-1]}p_{\ell-2}=0.$ Its denominator is nonzero by [F4]. Thus $E_m(J_m)=0=J_{m-1}$. This covers a seam contraction even when no two adjacent input endpoints of the projector are joined by a cap.

Denote by $\vartheta_t$ the planar curl of this auxiliary block crossing. Closing one strand gives $\vartheta_1=A\delta+A^{-1}=-A^3$. The cup/cap slides of step 1.2 give $\vartheta_{r+t}=C_{t,r}C_{r,t}(\vartheta_r\otimes\vartheta_t),\qquad \operatorname{ptr}_{t}(C_{t,t})=\vartheta_t,$ where $\operatorname{ptr}_t$ closes the last $t$ strands. Inclusion gives $J_n\otimes1\subseteq J_{n+1}$. We prove $E_n(J_n)\subseteq J_{n-1}$ by induction; below $m$ it is trivial and at $m$ it is step 2.1. With all $a_i,b_i\in B_{n-1}$ and $U=U_{n-1}$, the four types are $a_0fb_0$, $a_1Ua_2fb_0$, $a_0fb_1Ub_2$, and $a_1Ua_2fb_1Ub_2$. In the fourth, the induction hypothesis puts the middle factor in $J_{n-2}$, whose inclusion belongs to $J_{n-1}$, or is zero at the boundary. This proves trace closure. Iterated partial traces consequently carry $J_N$ into $J_n$ for every $n\le N$.

Fix arbitrary $a:t\to n$, $b:n\to t$ and $F=f\otimes1_{t-m}$, with $t\ge m$. Its middle factor equals $(f\otimes1_{N-m})(\vartheta_t^{-1}\otimes1_n)$, so $X\in J_N$. Naturality gives $(1_t\otimes b)C_{n,t}=C_{t,t}(b\otimes1_t)$, so also $X=(aF\vartheta_t^{-1}\otimes1_t)C_{t,t}(b\otimes1_t)$. Pulling maps on the untraced wires outside the closure and using step 2.2 now gives $\operatorname{ptr}_t(X)=aF\vartheta_t^{-1}\operatorname{ptr}_t(C_{t,t})b=aFb.$ By step 3.1 this belongs to $J_n$, even when $n<m$, where it is zero. A tensor-ideal word containing $f$ is a finite sum of composites $a(1_r\otimes f\otimes1_u)b$. If it contains further copies of $f$, expand those in their finite matching basis and absorb them into the multipliers, leaving one distinguished copy. Naturality with the auxiliary crossings moves $1_r\otimes f\otimes1_u$ to $f\otimes1_{r+u}$ by an invertible conjugation, absorbed in $a,b$. Conversely tensoring $f$ with identities and composing on either side puts the generators and all their two-sided multiples in $\mathcal I$. Hence $J_n\subseteq\mathcal I(n,n)$. Their equality and all partial-trace assertions follow, including the zero components below $m$.

derivations.claim: Work first over $\mathbb C(q)$. Let $V$ have ordered basis $(+, -)$, and define $w=+- -q^{-1}(-+)$ and $b(+,-)=-q$, $b(-,+)=1$, $b(+,+)=b(-,-)=0$. Direct evaluation on $+$ and $-$ gives both snakes $(1\otimes b)(w\otimes1)=1_V$ and $(b\otimes1)(1\otimes w)=1_V$, while $b(w)=-\delta$. Thus cup $\mapsto w$, cap $\mapsto b$ evaluates every planar diagram with loop $-\delta$: the two snake moves and deletion of a component have exactly their prescribed values, so the evaluation respects stacking and planar matching equality. This is a finite matrix evaluation of $\mathcal{TL}(-\delta)$, with no quantum-group input.

Write $e=wb$ and $U=-e$. In the two weight-zero words the nonzero block is $U|_{(+-, -+)}=\begin{pmatrix}q&-1\\-1&q^{-1}\end{pmatrix}$, which is symmetric under ordinary transpose. The generators $-e_i$ satisfy the positive-loop relations by the two snakes and $e_i^2=-\delta e_i$; consequently [F7] makes $U_i\mapsto-e_i$ an algebra isomorphism between the positive- and negative-loop diagram endomorphism algebras, with its own inverse of the same form.

Under loop $-\delta$, the quantum integers are $[j]_- =(-1)^{j-1}[j]$, by the recurrence in [F1]. Substitution in the JW recursion shows inductively that the isomorphism takes the positive projector $p_a$ to the negative-loop projector $p_a^-$. Its evaluated matrix $P_a$ is therefore the positive-loop JW recursion matrix built from the displayed symmetric $U$: it is symmetric, idempotent, annihilated by every $U_i$, and is identity plus nonempty $U$-words.

For a word $x$ of length $a$, let $j(x)$ count its minus signs, and let $\operatorname{inv}(x)$ count pairs consisting of a minus before a plus. Put $z_{a,j}=\sum_{j(x)=j}q^{\operatorname{inv}(x)}x$ and $Z_{a,j}=z_{a,j}^{\mathsf t}z_{a,j}=\sum_{j(x)=j}q^{2\operatorname{inv}(x)}$. The equation $U_iv=0$ says that the coefficient of a word with $-+$ in positions $i,i+1$ is $q$ times the coefficient of the otherwise identical word with $+-$ there. Adjacent swaps connect all words with fixed $j$, and replacing $+-$ by $-+$ increases inversion number by one. Hence the common kernel in that weight space is exactly $\mathbb C(q)z_{a,j}$. The image of $P_a$ lies in the common kernel; conversely its nonidentity generator words kill that kernel by their rightmost factor, so $P_a$ acts as identity there.

A symmetric rank-one projector with image $\mathbb C(q)z$ is $zz^{\mathsf t}/(z^{\mathsf t}z)$. Here $Z_{a,j}$ is a nonzero polynomial with constant term one, so it is invertible in $\mathbb C(q)$. Thus the actual JW matrix, rather than a substitute projector, has entries $ (P_a)_{x,y}=\frac{q^{\operatorname{inv}(x)+\operatorname{inv}(y)}}{Z_{a,j}}\quad\text{when }j(x)=j(y)=j. $ This includes $a=0$ with the empty word and $Z_{0,0}=1$.

Put $Q=q^2$ and write $\binom aj_Q$ for the Gaussian polynomial. Appending a plus to a word with $j$ minuses creates $j$ inversions, whereas appending a minus creates none. Therefore $Z_{a,j}=Q^jZ_{a-1,j}+Z_{a-1,j-1}$, with $Z_{a,0}=Z_{a,a}=1$. This is the Gaussian polynomial recurrence with the same initial values; induction gives $Z_{a,j}=\binom aj_Q$. Also $[u]=q^{1-u}(1+Q+\cdots+Q^{u-1})$, so conversion of the three factorials gives $Z_{a,j}=q^{j(a-j)}\frac{[a]!}{[j]![a-j]!}.$ All inversions here occur in $\mathbb C(q)$; root specialization will follow only after denominators have been put in the stated unit range.

The negative planar trace in this evaluation has pivotal matrix $J=-K$, where $K=\operatorname{diag}(q,q^{-1})$. Indeed the bilinear matrix of $b$ is $B_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&-q\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, and the symmetric planar transpose relation $JB_0^{\mathsf t}=B_0$ gives exactly $J=-K$; equivalently the corresponding direct cup/cap closure of a matrix $f$ is $\operatorname{Tr}((-K)f)$. Tensoring this closure gives $\operatorname{Tr}((-K)^{\otimes a}f)$ on $V^{\otimes a}$. The basis $z_{a,j}$ of $\operatorname{im}P_a$ has weights $a-2j$, so the negative-loop trace is $\dim_-(p_a)=(-1)^a\sum_{j=0}^aq^{a-2j}=(-1)^a[a+1].$ The diagram corner $p_t\operatorname{End}(t)p_t$ is scalar by [F2], also seen directly because an innermost turnback kills every nonidentity matching. The vector $+^t$ is fixed by $P_t$ and detects that scalar. Thus no faithfulness claim about arbitrary diagram Hom spaces is needed to recover the scalar used below.

Form the same $A,B,\alpha,\beta$ in the negative-loop diagram category, and denote the theta value by $\Theta_-$. For a word $x$ of length $m$, let $\bar x$ be its bitwise complement followed by reversal. The prescribed nested cups and caps give $W_m(1)=\sum_x(-q^{-1})^{j(x)}x\otimes\bar x,\qquad B_m(x\otimes\bar x)=(-q)^{m-j(x)},$ and $B_m$ is zero on other pairings of the two word bundles. This follows by multiplying the $m$ fundamental coefficients: a plus in $x$ contributes cup coefficient one and cap coefficient $-q$; a minus contributes cup coefficient $-q^{-1}$ and cap coefficient one. The reversed order is exactly the nesting in the Statement.

The negative-loop diagram $\beta\alpha$ is in the scalar $p_t$ corner, so write its evaluated matrix as $LP_t$. On $+^t$ the outer $P_t$ factors may be omitted: they fix this vector, all maps preserve total weight, and weight $t$ in $V^{\otimes t}$ is the one-dimensional space $\mathbb C(q)+^t$. Idempotence removes the doubled middle projectors. Hence $L$ is exactly the coefficient on $+^t$ obtained by applying $B(P_r\otimes P_s)A$ to $+^t$.

Let $x$ have $j$ minus signs and $v=\operatorname{inv}(x)$. Its $A$ output is $(+^px)\otimes(\bar x+^n)$ with coefficient $(-q^{-1})^j$. The two word inversion counts are $v$ and $v+(m-j)n$, since complement followed by reversal preserves inversions. Substitution in the actual projector entries of step 5.1, then summation over words with this fixed $j$, gives $(P_r\otimes P_s)A(+^t)=\sum_{j=0}^m C_j z_{r,j}\otimes z_{s,m-j},\qquad C_j=\frac{(-q^{-1})^j q^{(m-j)n}Z_{m,j}}{Z_{r,j}Z_{s,m-j}}.$ Here the sum of $q^{2v}$ over those words is precisely $Z_{m,j}$.

In applying $B$ to the $j$th tensor in step 10.1, only word pairs $(+^px,\bar x+^n)$ can leave all of its $p$ leftmost and $n$ rightmost through positions plus. Their contraction coefficient on $+^t$ is $(-q)^{m-j}q^{(m-j)n}Z_{m,j}$, by the same inversion count and the cap formula in step 8.1. Therefore every contraction is accounted for in $L=(-1)^m\sum_{j=0}^m q^{m-2j+2n(m-j)}\frac{Z_{m,j}^2}{Z_{m+p,j}Z_{m+n,m-j}}.$ This is an evaluation of the specified bundled, projector-labelled diagram, rather than an asserted strip identity.

Substituting step 6.1 into the quotient of $Z$ factors in step 11.1 contributes exponent $j(n-p)-mn$ and factorial factor $[m]!^2[m+p-j]![n+j]!/([m+p]![m+n]![j]![m-j]!)$. Consequently $L=\frac{(-1)^m[m]!^2}{[m+p]![m+n]!}S_{m,n,p},\qquad S_{m,n,p}=\sum_{j=0}^m q^{m(n+1)-j(n+p+2)}\frac{[m+p-j]![n+j]!}{[j]![m-j]!}.$ The exponent simplification is $m-2j+2n(m-j)+j(n-p)-mn=m(n+1)-j(n+p+2)$, so no omitted scalar or power of $q$ enters this norm contraction.

For $N\ge0$ the formal power series identity $\sum_{j\ge0}\binom{N+j}{j}_Qx^j=\prod_{i=0}^N(1-Q^ix)^{-1}$ follows coefficientwise. If $h_{N,j}$ denotes the right-hand coefficient, multiplying by $1-Q^Nx$ gives $h_{N,j}=h_{N-1,j}+Q^Nh_{N,j-1}$. The Gaussian polynomial on the left has the identical recurrence, since $\binom{N+j}{j}_Q=\binom{N+j-1}{j}_Q+Q^N\binom{N+j-1}{j-1}_Q$, and the initial values are $h_{0,j}=1$ and $h_{N,0}=1$. This Pascal identity follows by clearing the ordinary $Q$-factorial denominators, or by the inversion-word recurrence of step 6.1. Induction thus proves the displayed formal identity; there is no analytic convergence premise.

Apply step 13.1 to the adjacent exponent intervals $[-n-1,-1]$ and $[0,p]$. Their geometric-series products multiply to the product for the whole interval $[-n-1,p]$. The coefficient of $x^m$ is therefore $\sum_{j=0}^m Q^{-j(n+1)}\binom{n+j}{n}_Q\binom{p+m-j}{p}_Q=Q^{-m(n+1)}\binom{m+n+p+1}{m}_Q.$ The summand uses degree $j$ from the negative interval and degree $m-j$ from the nonnegative interval. Shifting all exponents of the combined interval up by $n+1$ and applying step 13.1 with $N=n+p+1$ gives the right side. This proves the finite q-Vandermonde identity used here.

Divide a summand of $S_{m,n,p}$ by $[n]![p]!$. Its factorial part is the product of the symmetric quantum binomials $\begin{bmatrix}m+p-j\\p\end{bmatrix}_q\begin{bmatrix}n+j\\n\end{bmatrix}_q$. Converting these to Gaussian polynomials by step 6.1 changes their combined prefactor to $q^{m(n+1-p)}Q^{-j(n+1)}$. Thus step 14.1 gives the symmetric binomial $q^{-m(n+p+1)}\binom{h+1}{m}_Q=\begin{bmatrix}h+1\\m\end{bmatrix}_q$ after this same conversion, and hence $S_{m,n,p}=\frac{[n]![p]![h+1]!}{[m]![n+p+1]!}.$ Substitution into step 12.1 proves $L=\frac{(-1)^m[m]![n]![p]![h+1]!}{[m+p]![m+n]![n+p+1]!}.$ Every sum and exponent in this evaluation has therefore been derived independently of a theta formula or recoupling coefficient.

The negative diagram satisfies $\Theta_-=(-1)^t[t+1]L$ by step 7.1. To compare it with the desired positive-loop theta, expand all three projectors as generator words. Under $U_i\mapsto-e_i$, a term with a total of $v$ generator insertions gains coefficient sign $(-1)^v$, by step 3.1. With no insertions its closed matching has exactly $h=m+t$ circles: $m$ cup/cap circles and $t$ through-strand closures. One cup-cap insertion reconnects two edges of a closed planar one-manifold and merges two components or splits one; thus it changes the circle count by $\pm1$. Consequently the total count $c$ for a term with $v$ insertions satisfies $c\equiv h+v\pmod2$, including components removed during stacking. Evaluating its loops at $-\delta$ gives sign $(-1)^c$, so its combined sign is always $(-1)^{v+c}=(-1)^h$. Summing the terms proves the diagrammatic identity $\Theta_-=(-1)^h\Theta$, without presupposing a factorial evaluation.

Since $h+t\equiv m\pmod2$, steps 15.1 and 16.1 give $\Theta=(-1)^m[t+1]L=\frac{[m]![n]![p]![h+1]!}{[m+n]![n+p]![m+p]!}.$ At $p=0$ this is $[m+n+1]$, which checks the stated normalization: there is no extra sign, dimension, or scalar at a vertex.

The proved scalar expression gives the cross-multiplied closed-diagram strip identity $[m+p][n+p]\Theta(m,n,p)=[p][m+n+p+1]\Theta(m,n,p-1)$ for $p\ge1$. This is an identity of the specifically defined diagrams' evaluations because steps 1.1–17.1 derived their JW entries, nested cup/cap contractions, exponent factors, and finite sum. A pictorial strip manipulation or the theta recurrence has not been assumed as a premise. Over $\mathbb C(q)$ its unit factors can be divided to give $\Theta(m,n,p)/\Theta(m,n,p-1)=[p][m+n+p+1]/([m+p][n+p])$. Starting with $\Theta(m,n,0)=[m+n+1]$, the product telescopes as $[m+n+1]\prod_{j=1}^p\frac{[j][m+n+j+1]}{[m+j][n+j]}=\frac{[m]![n]![p]![h+1]!}{[m+n]![m+p]![n+p]!}.$ The analogous strip recurrence in $m$ or $n$ follows by relabelling the three bundles or by the proved symmetric expression.

Each JW recursion coefficient is a rational Laurent function with denominators products of $[j]$ for $j\le M=\max(r,s,t)$, by [F2]. The actual theta diagram therefore belongs to the localization $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1},[1]^{-1},\ldots,[M]^{-1}]$. The right side of step 17.1 is in the same localization, since its only denominators are $[r]![s]![t]!$. Their equality over $\mathbb C(q)$ is consequently an equality in that localization and specializes at every point where these quantum integers are units, even if an intermediate norm formula or a quotient of two theta values has a zero denominator there. This specializes the final identity, rather than dividing a zero theta value at the root. The Laurent-polynomial convention of [F1] also covers $q=\pm1$.

Now let $q=e^{\pi i/\ell}$, $\ell\ge3$, and $0\le r,s,t\le\ell-2$. Every denominator index is at most $\ell-2$, so its quantum integer is nonzero. If $h\le\ell-2$, all numerator indices are at most $\ell-1$, and $[j]=\sin(j\pi/\ell)/\sin(\pi/\ell)>0$ in this range, so $\Theta>0$. If $h\ge\ell-1$, then $[h+1]!$ contains $[\ell]=0$, while the denominator remains nonzero, so $\Theta=0$. This uses no division by $[\ell]$ and no $0/0$ limit, and covers even $\ell$ and $\ell=3$. Labels outside a domain in which their required JW projectors exist are not unqualified root diagrams.

Finally sandwich any matching $t\to r+s$ by $p_t$ and $p_r\otimes p_s$. If an arc joins two points on the same labelled arm, its innermost turnback is killed by that arm's projector. The only remaining noncrossing matching is the stated $m,n,p$-bundled vertex. Thus its projected Hom space is spanned by $\alpha$, and the reverse space by $\beta$, over the root field as well as generically. Their entire trace pairing is scalar multiplication by $\Theta$. Nonzero $\Theta$ makes that vertex pairing nondegenerate; zero $\Theta$ makes the vertex have zero trace pairing against every reverse morphism, including an arbitrary reverse map after inserting the projectors and using cyclicity. This proves the stated root pairing conclusions without dividing by a forbidden-level theta value. Together with steps 17.1 and 18.1–20.1, it proves all claims.

Let $R$ be a nonzero commutative ring with unit, $\delta\in R$, and suppose $[2],\ldots,[n]$ are units. The projector $p_n$ of [[def-temperley-lieb-jones-wenzl-recursion-over-unit-denominators]] has coefficient $1$ on the identity diagram, is nonzero and idempotent, and is annihilated on both sides by each $U_i$ for $1\le i<n$. Its corner is $p_n\mathrm{TL}_n p_n=R p_n$, so it is the unique idempotent with identity coefficient $1$ and those two-sided annihilation conditions. For $n\ge1$,

$$\operatorname{ptr}_n(p_n)=\frac{[n+1]}{[n]}p_{n-1},\qquad \operatorname{Tr}_n(p_n)=[n+1].$$

Only the displayed denominator units are assumed; $\delta$ need not be a unit.

For any commutative ring $R$, loop value $\delta\in R$, and $n\ge0$, the unnormalized trace of [[def-temperley-lieb-closure-trace-and-partial-trace]] satisfies

$$\operatorname{Tr}_n(xy)=\operatorname{Tr}_n(yx),\qquad \operatorname{Tr}_{n+1}(x\otimes1)=\delta\operatorname{Tr}_n(x),\qquad \operatorname{Tr}_{n+1}((x\otimes1)U_n)=\operatorname{Tr}_n(x)$$

for $x,y\in\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$, where $U_n$ is the cup-cap generator on the last two strands of $\mathrm{TL}_{n+1}$. For $x\in\mathrm{TL}_{n-1}$ and $h\in\mathrm{TL}_n$,

$$\operatorname{Tr}_n\bigl(h(x\otimes1)\bigr)=\operatorname{Tr}_{n-1}\bigl(\operatorname{ptr}_n(h)x\bigr).$$

No division by $\delta$ occurs.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and let $\delta\in R$. The object labels are the nonnegative integers $n=0,1,2,\ldots$. For labels $m,n$, place bottom points $b_1,\ldots,b_m$ and top points $t_1,\ldots,t_n$ along the rectangle from left to right on their respective edges. Their cyclic order is $t_1,\ldots,t_n,b_m,\ldots,b_1$. When $m=n=0$, the empty matching is included.

An $(m,n)$ **diagram** is a perfect matching of these $m+n$ boundary labels which is noncrossing: there are no four labels $a,b,c,d$ in cyclic order whose matched pairs are $\{a,c\}$ and $\{b,d\}$. A picture consists of disjoint arcs realizing the matching; equality is equality of the matching, so planar deformation that fixes the boundary does not change a diagram. If $m+n$ is odd, there are no such diagrams. Write $\mathcal D(m,n)$ for this set and define the $R$-module

$$M_R(m,n):=R^{(\mathcal D(m,n))},$$

the free $R$-module on the set of diagrams ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]). In particular, its diagram basis is empty when $m+n$ is odd.

For basis diagrams $D:m\to n$ and $E:n\to p$, stack $E$ above $D$ and identify the $n$ matching boundary points. The resulting finite graph has degree two at each identified point, where degree means the number of incident arcs. Each component is a path joining two exterior boundary points or a closed cycle. Remove every cycle and multiply the remaining exterior matching by $\delta^c$, where $c$ is the number of removed cycles. Denote this output by $E\circ D$ and extend the rule $R$-bilinearly to a map $M_R(n,p)\times M_R(m,n)\to M_R(m,p)$. A following result proves closure of these operations on the diagram modules and the category axioms.

The matching $1_n:n\to n$ pairs each bottom point to the top point directly above it. Horizontal juxtaposition, with the left diagram placed first, defines $m\otimes m'=m+m'$ on object labels and $D\otimes D'$ on basis diagrams; extend it $R$-bilinearly to the modules. A following result proves that these operations give a strict monoidal category.

For $1\le i<n$, let $d_i\in M_R(n,n)$ be the diagram with a cap joining top points $i,i+1$, a cup joining bottom points $i,i+1$, and vertical through strands at every other position. Define $\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$ to be the $R$-module $M_R(n,n)$ with bilinear multiplication $xy:=x\circ y$ and distinguished element $1_n$. A following result proves that it is a unital associative $R$-algebra and identifies it with the endomorphism algebra at object $n$.

The left factor is stacked above the right factor. The loop value is $\delta$; no invertibility or nonzero condition on $\delta$ is part of these data.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit and $\delta\in R$. Define the quantum integers by

$$[0]_\delta=0,\qquad [1]_\delta=1,\qquad [r+1]_\delta=\delta[r]_\delta-[r-1]_\delta\quad(r\ge1).$$

The **quantum characteristic** of $(R,\delta)$ is the least positive integer $\ell$ with $[\ell]_\delta=0$, if one exists, and $\ell=\infty$ otherwise. No element of $R$ is inverted in this definition.

For $q\in\mathbb C^\times$ and $\delta=q+q^{-1}$, write $[r]_q=[r]_\delta$. If $q\ne\pm1$, this agrees with $(q^r-q^{-r})/(q-q^{-1})$; at $q=\pm1$ the recurrence gives $[r]_q=rq^{r-1}$. For complex-parameter classification, write $\kappa=\operatorname{ord}(q^2)$, with $\kappa=\infty$ when $q^2$ has infinite order. If $q\ne\pm1$, the quantum characteristic equals $\kappa$ when $\kappa<\infty$ and is $\infty$ otherwise. At $q=\pm1$, $\kappa=1$ but the complex quantum characteristic is $\infty$, because $[r]_q=rq^{r-1}\ne0$ for every positive $r$.

For a field $K$ of positive characteristic $p$, set $p(0)=1$ and, when $\ell<\infty$, set $p(i)=\ell p^{i-1}$ for $i\ge1$. In characteristic zero and finite $\ell$, the finite digit scale is $p(1)=\ell$; the separate characteristic-zero criterion below uses $a\ell-1$ for arbitrary positive integers $a$. If $\ell=\infty$, every finite index is already in the range $n<\ell$.

Initially let $q$ be an indeterminate, let $[j]=q^{j-1}+q^{j-3}+\cdots+q^{1-j}$ for $j\ge1$, let $[0]!=1$, and set $\delta=q+q^{-1}$. For nonnegative integers $m,n,p$, put
$$r=m+p,\qquad s=m+n,\qquad t=n+p,\qquad h=m+n+p.$$
Equivalently, $(r,s,t)$ satisfies the triangle inequalities and even-sum condition, with $m=(r+s-t)/2$, $n=(s+t-r)/2$, and $p=(t+r-s)/2$. All Jones–Wenzl projectors below have identity coefficient one and are unnormalized.

Let $W_m:0\to2m$ be $m$ nested cups, whose outputs are two consecutive $m$-strand bundles: cup $i$ joins position $i$ of the first bundle to position $m+1-i$ of the second. Let $B_m:2m\to0$ be its horizontal reflection. Define
$$A=1_p\otimes W_m\otimes1_n:t\longrightarrow r+s,\qquad B=1_p\otimes B_m\otimes1_n:r+s\longrightarrow t,$$
$$\alpha=(p_r\otimes p_s)Ap_t,\qquad \beta=p_tB(p_r\otimes p_s),\qquad \Theta(m,n,p)=\operatorname{Tr}_t(\beta\alpha).$$
Thus the pairwise bundles at each trivalent vertex have sizes $m,n,p$: there are $m$ strands between arms $r,s$, $n$ between arms $s,t$, and $p$ between arms $t,r$. This fixes the vertex without a further scalar normalization. The theta net has the three JW-labelled edges $r,s,t$, since idempotence collapses the doubled projectors. Its value is
$$\Theta(m,n,p)=\frac{[m]![n]![p]![h+1]!}{[m+n]![n+p]![m+p]!}.$$
For $p\ge1$ the closed-diagram strip recurrence is
$$[m+p][n+p]\Theta(m,n,p)=[p][m+n+p+1]\Theta(m,n,p-1),\qquad \Theta(m,n,0)=[m+n+1].$$

These identities specialize to every complex $q\ne0$ for which $[j]\ne0$ for $1\le j\le M=\max(r,s,t)$, using the Laurent-polynomial convention at $q=\pm1$. These hypotheses construct the three projectors and make every displayed denominator a unit; $[h+1]$ need not be nonzero. In particular, if $q=e^{\pi i/\ell}$, $\ell\ge3$, and $0\le r,s,t\le\ell-2$, then $\Theta>0$ when $h\le\ell-2$, whereas $\Theta=0$ when $h\ge\ell-1$. The latter vertex has zero trace pairing against every reverse morphism. No undefined higher root projector or $0/0$ convention is used.

Let $q=e^{\pi i/\ell}$, $\ell\ge3$, $\delta=q+q^{-1}$, $m=\ell-1$ and $f=p_m$. Put $B_n=\mathrm{TL}_n(\mathbb C,\delta)$ and

$$J_n=\begin{cases}0,&n<m,\\ B_n(f\otimes1_{n-m})B_n,&n\ge m.\end{cases}$$

If $\mathcal I$ is the categorical tensor ideal generated by $f$, then $\mathcal I(n,n)=J_n$ at every rank. Moreover $\operatorname{ptr}_n(J_n)\subseteq J_{n-1}$. Thus this single embedded two-sided ideal already contains every annular consequence with arbitrary external strands and cups/caps. Below the boundary its component is zero, including contractions given by a partial trace rather than an internal turnback.

In the pivotal setting of [[def-negligible-morphism-in-a-pivotal-category]], the negligible morphisms are closed under addition, scalar multiplication, arbitrary composition on either side, and tensor product on either side. Thus they form a two-sided tensor ideal. The proof uses an explicit partial-trace identity and does not assume that an arbitrary intertwiner of a tensor product factors as a tensor product of intertwiners.

derivations.claim: The theta formula and exact vertex convention are [F4]. At a retained triangle/parity triple, its denominator indices are $r,s,t\le\ell-2$. If $h=(r+s+t)/2\le\ell-2$, every numerator index is at most $\ell-1$ and [F3] makes the ratio positive. If $h\ge\ell-1$, its numerator factorial $[h+1]!$ contains $[\ell]$, whereas the denominator stays nonzero; its value is zero. These conclusions specialize the generic localization identity, not a ratio of theta values at the root.

For $1\le a\le k$ set $f_a=p_a\otimes1$, $X_a=f_aU_af_a$ and $\lambda_a=[a+1]/[a]$. Define $\alpha_a=f_a(1_{a-1}\otimes\cup)p_{a-1},\qquad \beta_a=p_{a-1}(1_{a-1}\otimes\cap)f_a.$ Absorption of $p_{a-1}$ next to $p_a$ gives $\alpha_a\beta_a=X_a$: insert the cup/cap and remove the absorbed lower projector. Closing the other composite is exactly the right partial trace of $p_a$ in its lower corner, so [F1] gives $\beta_a\alpha_a=\lambda_ap_{a-1}$. Thus $X_a^2=\lambda_aX_a$. The JW recursion gives $f_a=p_{a+1}+\lambda_a^{-1}\alpha_a\beta_a.$ The two terms are orthogonal because $p_{a+1}$ kills the joining turnback. The down maps are inclusion $\alpha_a$ and retraction $\lambda_a^{-1}\beta_a$; the up maps are the tautological inclusion/retraction of $p_{a+1}$. For $a=0$ there is only $p_1$. Every denominator here has index at most $\ell-1$ and is nonzero.

For retained endpoints, $\operatorname{Hom}(p_a,p_b)=0$ if $a\ne b$ and is $\mathbb Cp_a$ if $a=b$. Indeed any matching between unequal boundaries has an innermost adjacent cap or cup at the larger boundary and is killed by its JW projector. Between equal boundaries, every nonidentity matching has such a turnback. The identity corner survives in the quotient: its trace is $[a+1]>0$, while the boundary tensor ideal is negligible. For the latter assertion, $p_{k+1}$ has one-dimensional endomorphism corner and trace $[\ell]=0$, so every test trace vanishes; tensor-ideal closure in [F5] gives the assertion at all objects. Thus the quotient introduces no extra identification in the retained scalar corners.

At $a=k$, pass to the categorical quotient and delete $p_{k+1}$ from the decomposition before taking any further normalization. The identity becomes $p_k\otimes1=\lambda_k^{-1}\alpha_k\beta_k$ with $\lambda_k=[\ell-1]/[\ell-2]\ne0$. It therefore has only its down summand. In particular at $\ell=3$, $k=1$, this says that the quotient tensor square is its trivial channel; no retained highest-weight-$2$ summand is asserted. The endomorphism ideal being killed is exactly [F5]'s embedded one.

Start with the single rank-zero path and tensor its identity decomposition by $1$. Inductively split each endpoint summand $p_a\otimes1$ by steps 1.2 and 2.1 and compose its up/down maps with the preceding path maps. Cross-composites of the new up/down terms vanish by turnback annihilation; the equal down composite is $\lambda_a^{-1}\beta_a\alpha_a=p_{a-1}$ and the up composite is $p_{a+1}$. Different preceding paths have zero composite by induction. Their new projections sum to the old projection tensored with $1$, because the split is complete; at the boundary only the down term remains. This proves simultaneously $r_ai_b=0$ for distinct paths, $r_ai_a=p_{a_n}$ and $\sum_a i_ar_a=1_n$ for every rank.

For paths with equal endpoint put $E_{a,b}=i_ar_b$. The composites in step 3.1 give their matrix-unit multiplication. Insert the complete path identity on each side of any morphism and use the corners of step 1.3: these units span all endomorphisms, and the same argument describes unequal-degree Hom spaces. They are independent because multiplying a putative relation by $r_a$ and $i_b$ isolates its coefficient times the nonzero endpoint projector. Closing $i_ar_b$ has the same finite component graph as closing $r_bi_a$, even though the cut occurs at a different object. Thus the trace is zero off the diagonal and $[a_n+1]$ on it. Each matrix block has nonzero weighted ordinary trace pairing, detected by its transposed matrix units. This proves completeness and nondegeneracy at every rank. Together with step 1.1 it proves all assertions without a recoupling division at the boundary.
